#4545. Mind Games: My ‘Secret’ to Enjoying Coffee Without Anxiety

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A guide to therapy, medications, and techniques for managing anxiety

Nutrition tips and tools for supporting mental well-being

Resources for finding and receiving therapy

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

This article is part of a mental health content series called “Mind Games,” in which Healthline editor Morgan Mandriota draws on personal experience and research to challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma, review trends, and share hot takes and lessons learned about what it means to be mentally well.

Coffee and I don’t exactly have the best relationship.

My morning cup tends to give me jitters, worsen my anxiety, and keep me up until 2 a.m. if I drink it past noon. As an already anxious human, the last thing I need is to exacerbate my symptoms, even if it’s coming from a delicious source.

Over a year ago, I noticed that my anxiety was higher than usual. I was also tossing and turning and waking up at all hours of the night for weeks on end.

One night in particular, I woke up every hour for 8 hours. Naturally, I wanted to blame it on the full moon or anything other than my beloved coffee, but alas, I realized that my caffeine consumption was the most likely culprit.

Could I have aimed to set a strict drinking schedule to see if that fixed things? Sure. But instead, I decided to quit cold turkey and undergo an experiment to see how I’d feel going coffee-free for the first time in years.

Over the next 8 months, I’d swap my coffee station for a matcha setup, dabble in exotic herbal blends from my local teahouse, and become a self-proclaimed tea connoisseur. Lo and behold, my anxiety eased up, and my sleep quality improved, too.

Fast forward to 4 months ago, when I hopped back on the coffee train. But this time, I’m relying on a handy amino acid to help avoid anxiety and other unwanted side effects: L-theanine.

Health and wellness touch everyone’s life differently. This is one person’s story. The views and opinions expressed are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Healthline Media and should not serve as a substitute for medical advice from a healthcare professional.

L-theanine is mainly found in green and black tea and one type of wild mushroom. The mental health benefits of L-theanine consumption are an emerging area of research, but one 2024 review found that consuming around 200 to 400 milligrams (mg) may help relieve symptoms in people with anxiety disorders.

Still, anecdotal reports suggest there may be benefits of adding L-theanine to coffee. Over the last 5 years, the combo has been gaining traction on Reddit and TikTok for managing caffeine-related side effects.

Despite an overwhelming amount of rave reviews online, I couldn’t find much research to support these claims, so I spoke with a neurologist to see if they had any thoughts.

“This trend has real science behind it,” said Fawad Mian, MD, who is board certified in neurology, clinical neurophysiology, and sleep medicine and the founder of Ascend Regenerative.

“Controlled studies show caffeine plus L-theanine improves focus and attention more than caffeine alone, and some suggest it softens caffeine’s side effects, like tiredness, headaches, and blood pressure spikes,” Mian said. “It smooths caffeine’s effects but doesn’t erase them, so it’s not a license to drink more coffee,” he added.

With all of this in mind, especially after realizing just how calm I was while drinking black and green teas during my coffee break, I decided to give it a try.

After about 4 months of “testing,” I’ve found that adding L-theanine to my coffee works extremely well for me.

No more anxiety, scatterbrain, shakiness, or staying up until 3 a.m. And no lifestyle overhaul needed. The supplement, which I prefer in liquid form, has become a seamless addition to my daily routine.

Every morning, I make a fresh batch of French press coffee with (strong) local beans, then I squeeze some L-theanine into my cup.

I’ve noticed that I get the usual coffee benefits like improved focus and concentration, plus a nice, calm, stable energy throughout the day.

Even if I drink it until 2 p.m., I’m fighting to keep my eyes open at night before I finally fall asleep around 10. Perhaps this is because L-theanine may also support quality sleep.

Mindful L-Theanine Drops is the liquid supplement that I use every day.

I add a one-second squeeze (which contains 200 mg of L-theanine) into my morning coffee, then I’m good to go. I even started carrying a bottle in my bag just in case I get a latte from a coffee shop on a whim.

You can also add it to a glass of water, a cup of tea, or another drink of your choosing. It’s unflavored, so it doesn’t alter the taste of your drinks. Real secret stuff.

Out of curiosity, and because I’m a natural skeptic and overthinker, I asked Mian if my positive experience could be a placebo effect, or if I’m seeing real results.

“Expectation may play a small role, but the effect is biologically plausible,” he said. “L-theanine boosts calming brain activity that offsets caffeine’s stimulation, and 200 mg matches the doses used in studies.” However, he noted that it doesn’t speed caffeine clearance, so drinking coffee only in the morning still matters for sleep quality.

While L-theanine is generally safe to consume, it’s best to speak with a healthcare professional first, especially if you’re pregnant, nursing, receiving cancer treatment, or taking blood pressure medication or sedatives.

“Choose a third-party tested brand, and if caffeine makes you anxious, cutting back is still the simplest fix,” Mian added.

So, if you’re anything like me and drinking coffee also leads to anxiety and jitters for you, I highly recommend trying this supplement once you get the green light from your doctor. It’s been working for me. It may work well for you, too.

#4544. BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design

A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender. Breaking the injunction costs BYD €100,000 per day, up to €10 million.

It’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight. BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday before closing 1.9% lower.

The preliminary relief judge at the District Court of The Hague issued the ruling on Friday, November 20, in summary proceedings JLR brought against 11 BYD companies.

JLR put six registered EU designs in front of the court. The judge only needed one of them: design 005248580-0004, registered in April 2018 and covering the current Defender 110, known internally as the L663.

According to the ruling, the elements that dominate that design are the rounded “shoulders,” the rounded corners, the signature panel on the C-pillar, the rounded wheel-arch cutouts, the continuous window line, and the overall silhouette. The court found every one of them on the Ti7.

Here’s how the two SUVs compare from the same angles, using official press images from BYD and JLR:

BYD argued that the headlights, grille, bumpers, hood and side profile are all different. Not enough, said the judge, who ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression. The court also found the Ti7 sits closer to the Defender than to older boxy SUVs like the Ford Flex, Jeep Wrangler and Mercedes G-Class.

BYD doesn’t sell the Ti7 in the EU. It told the court it has “no concrete plans” to launch it there and that the SUV can only be ordered in the UK.

The judge didn’t buy that as a defense. By BYD’s own account, it developed the seven-seat layout for the UK and Europe, a promotional video called the Ti7 the first seven-seat SUV “in Europe,” and BYD wouldn’t commit to keeping it out of the EU. That was enough for the court to find a threat of infringement.

So BYD’s EU entities can no longer import, produce, offer, sell, store or supply the Ti7. The order kicks in one week after the ruling is formally served, and it even covers BYD’s Hungarian unit, since the judge considered it conceivable the Ti7 could come out of the new Szeged factory.

The UK is a different story. The court said it has no jurisdiction over BYD UK and threw out JLR’s UK design claims, so British deliveries are still on for January 2027. That’s the one European market where BYD actually opened orders, pricing the Ti7 at £47,995, about £24,000 below the £71,840 plug-in Defender 110.

BYD said it “strongly disagrees” with the judgment and will appeal, adding that the Ti7 “is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights.” JLR told AFP it protects its intellectual property and takes legal action when necessary.

BYD has four weeks to appeal, but the injunction stays in force while it does. JLR, for its part, has six months to file a full case on the merits, or BYD can get the injunction lifted.

There’s more coming. JLR also has a separate case in Rotterdam over copyright and “slavish imitation,” with a hearing scheduled for Wednesday.

This whole thing started in August, when JLR had bailiffs raid BYD’s Dutch offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. The court later ordered JLR to destroy everything it seized, saying it didn’t need BYD’s internal files to make its design case. And it didn’t. JLR won on the design registration alone.

The Ti7 looks like a Defender. We said so when BYD first brought it to the UK, and so did pretty much everyone else. Chinese automakers have been building Defender lookalikes for years, but most of them stayed in China.

BYD brought one to the Defender’s home turf at a £24,000 discount, so a fight with JLR was always coming.

"...ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression."

Really? I feel like anyone who pays even a little attention to car designs isn't going to mistake the two. The thing most people see as differentiating within the same category is the headlights, tail lights, grill - which are all significantly different.

The only real similarity is the proportions, there are a ton of similarly proportioned SUVs but that's a result of the form factor.

But honestly, all these boxy SUVs look the same to me.

Nobody owns “boxy.” JLR even failed to trademark the classic Defender’s shape in the UK, a fight it lost in its legal battle with the Ineos Grenadier. But it registered the new Defender’s design in 2018, and that specific combination of shoulders, C-pillar panel and wheel arches is exactly what the court protected. That’s how design rights are supposed to work.

The actual business damage is small for now. The Ti7 sells roughly 30,000 units a month, almost all in China, and the UK launch goes ahead. The stock dip was about headlines more than lost Ti7 sales.

Sony’s flagship noise-cancelling headphones are a frequent traveler’s best friend.

If you’re shopping for a flagship, the WH-1000XM6 is the pair to grab whether you fly, commute, or work somewhere loud. Sony’s QN3 processor drives the noise cancellation, and the earcups fold again, so the headphones pack smaller than the XM5 ever did. In our first impressions, they fixed the last generation’s biggest flaw and sounded better doing it.

Bose’s everyday noise-canceling headphones offer great features for less than a flagship.

The QuietComfort Headphones are the pair to recommend to anyone who wants excellent noise cancellation without paying flagship prices. You can switch between Quiet and Aware modes or build a custom mode in the Bose app, and multipoint Bluetooth keeps them connected to a phone and a laptop at the same time. Bose rates the battery at 24 hours, and the included audio cable means you can still plug into a seatback screen on a flight.

If you live in Apple’s ecosystem, the Beats Studio Pro drop to $139.95 (was $299.99) and add lossless USB-C audio for wired listening. You’ll also find options from some of our favorite brands, including Sony, Sennheiser, and Bowers & Wilkins.

The Nothing Ear (3) earbuds hit $99 (was $149) and bring hybrid noise cancellation and app-based EQ to the mid-price tier. Runners and cyclists who need to hear traffic should look at the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2, which leave your ear canals open for situational awareness while you sweat and currently only cost $119.95 (was $199.95). See our guide to the best earbuds for more help picking a pair.

A powerful, IP65 PA-style speaker that still manages to be portable at 21.4 compact pounds.

Plus, it’s easy to transport with the built-in corner handle. And the battery should easily outlast your party if you keep things at mid-volume, but it’s also swappable, and extras are currently $159. And if you really want to make things exciting, top the speaker(s) with a $199 3.86-pound LIGHTBOKS that pulses to the beat.

A rugged, floating Bluetooth speaker for under $100.

The Bose SoundLink Flex (2nd Gen.) is small enough to clip to a backpack and tough enough to survive a drop in the lake, since it carries an IP67 rating and floats. Bose kept the 12-hour battery from the original and added AAC and aptX Adaptive support, so both iPhone and Android owners get a better Bluetooth connection than the first model’s SBC-only setup. A customizable shortcut button handles tasks like pairing a second speaker. At $99, it grabs your attention for more than sonic reasons. And for more picks, see our guide to the best portable Bluetooth speakers.

Alternately, the Marshall Emberton III is a palm-sized powerhouse at $89.99 (was $179.99), and its amp-inspired design is rated IP67 against dust and water. For a bigger sound at a backyard party, the Sony ULT Field 5 falls to $188 (was $349.99) … and the bigger, punchier ULT Tower 5 is $299. Those are just two of the two dozen amazing options listed below.

The beyerdynamic DT 770 Pro has been a fixture in recording studios since the mid-1980s, and it works just as well for everyday listening at home. The closed-back design keeps outside noise out and your music in, while the plush velour pads stay comfortable through long sessions. The 80-ohm version runs fine from a laptop or phone, though one of the DACs below will give it more headroom, making them a great buy at $139.99.

The beyerdynamic DT 990 Pro is the open-back sibling of the DT 770 Pro above, and it drops to $139.99 (was $199.99). Its wide, airy soundstage suits mixing and critical listening, though the 250-ohm version really wants a dedicated headphone amp. On the in-ear side, the 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 remain one of the best ways to hear what wired IEMs can do for about $21. Our list of the best mixing headphones can give you more studio insight.

The WiiM Ultra adds Wi-Fi streaming, a touchscreen, and an ESS DAC to any stereo, and it drops to $296.65 (was $349). For headphones, the Fosi Audio K7 desktop DAC and amp is just $169.98 (was $199.99), and it’s a sensible first upgrade for anyone moving past a laptop’s headphone jack. Those are just a couple of components available to build a better listening station.

A one-button turntable that plays nice with Bluetooth speakers and real stereos.

The PS-LX3BT is an easy first step up from a suitcase record player. Press play, and it lowers the tonearm, finds the groove, and returns the arm when the side ends, so you never have to cue the record by hand. A switchable built-in phono preamp lets it connect to powered speakers or an amp without extra gear, and aptX Adaptive Bluetooth sends your records to wireless headphones or speakers. At $238, it’s well under the cap on our list of the best turntables under $500.

If the PS-LX3BT above leaves you wanting more, the Sony PS-LX5BT is Sony’s step-up model with more premium components but still a nice price at $398 (was $499.99). Pair either turntable with the Klipsch R-41M bookshelf speakers at $134.47 (was $199) and an amp from the section above for a complete starter system (Klipsch is just one solid option for turntable speakers).

Want to go digital? There are a ton of smart, whole-home, streaming-friendly connected speakers on sale below. We love a compact listening station.

The Sonos Arc Ultra drops to $849 (was $1,099) and delivers Dolby Atmos from a single bar that also anchors a whole-home Sonos system. For a smaller TV or a tighter budget, the Bose TV Speaker is $199 (was $279) and is built to make dialogue easier to follow than a TV’s built-in speakers.

#4541. Mink braves bears to find food, wins award

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 24, 2026 5:10 PM EST

In a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species. For its tenacity in finding food, a small mink (Neogale vison)  walking around Anan Creek wins the On a Mission Award.

“This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write. “It seemed unconcerned by nearby humans, completely focused on the small crabs and other nibbles it could get ahold of. It was on a mission to eat!”

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive the long winter ahead. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own antics and quirks.

In addition to the bears and mink, numerous other animals call Tongass home. Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), the Alexander Archipelago wolf (Canis lupus ligoni), and the Sitka black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis). Importantly, all five of North America’s Pacific salmon species are found within the forest—Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), coho (Oncorhynchus kisutch), pink (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), sockeye  (Oncorhynchus nerka), and chum (Oncorhynchus keta). These five fish species help feed the bears and other mammals and birds who gather here.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4540. How to Plan Your Holiday Meals in a Year of Unprecedented Recalls

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Following a series of high-profile food recalls and outbreaks this year, many Americans may be concerned about keeping their families safe from foodborne illness during the holidays.

In fact, according to a recent national survey by Orlando Health, around 60% of U.S. adults say they’re more concerned about foodborne illness this year than in previous years.

Although several major foodborne illness outbreaks have ended and their associated recalls are no longer active, food safety remains an important concern. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that 48 million people in the United States experience foodborne illness each year.

However, there are simple steps you can take to reduce the risk of foodborne illness when preparing holiday meals and storing leftovers.

While there were several food recalls in the United States over the summer, two of the largest involved Salmonella linked to jalapeños and Cyclospora linked to lettuce.

These outbreaks prompted widespread recalls and raised concerns about the safety of certain foods, particularly fresh produce.

Although health officials have since declared the major outbreaks over, some consumers may still be hesitant to purchase foods associated with previous recalls.

Even with this declaration, you may still feel nervous about purchasing certain foods, but experts say you don’t need to worry.

“Here in the United States, we have the safest food supply in the world. The recent recalls show that our food safety system is working,” said William Schaffner, MD, Professor, Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University.

Michelle Routhenstein, preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished, told Healthline that past recalls do not mean entire food categories need to be avoided. The important thing is whether the specific product you have matches a current recall, based on details such as brand, lot number, package size, and expiration date.

“You should enjoy familiar foods, including properly cooked poultry, washed fruits and vegetables, and pasteurized dairy products,” she said. “The key is checking relevant recalls and practicing safe food handling.”

“Before shopping or cooking, review FDA and USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) recall information and compare any relevant notices with the labels on your ingredients,” said Routhenstein.

Check the pantry and freezer, too: something purchased months ago may still be affected.

“Stay alert to any news reports about food recalls and use good food preparation practices. Those simple actions should keep your holidays happy and safe,” said Schaffner.

Consumers can sign up for food recall alerts through the FDA or visit FoodSafety.gov for recall information from both the FDA and USDA.

Schaffner emphasized the importance of following safe food-handling practices when preparing everyday meals and holiday gatherings.

“Remember the longstanding advice: keep food hot or cold. Avoid long times at room temperature,” he said.

Routhenstein advised focusing on four basics: clean, separate, cook, and chill.

Schaffner noted the importance of refrigerating leftovers promptly rather than leaving them at room temperature for extended periods. He recommends clearing the table and refrigerating leftovers soon after the meal ends.

Routhenstein reiterated that you should refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours rather than leaving them out to cool.

Divide turkey into smaller portions and transfer sides and gravy into shallow containers to help them cool quickly, she advised.

Leftovers can typically be stored in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. If you don’t plan to eat them within that time, consider freezing them.

The important thing is to keep an eye out for any new recalls, practice food safety, and enjoy your holiday meals!

#4538. Subaru is cutting EV prices by dropping one of its most distinctive features

Subaru vehicles are known for their dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) capabilities, but to cut costs, the company is now offering front-wheel-drive (FWD) versions on select electric models.

The Uncharted EV went on sale earlier this year as a smaller, sportier entry-level electric crossover positioned below the Solterra.

It was also the first Subaru model in about 30 years not to come with standard all-wheel drive. After unveiling the Uncharted EV last summer, Subaru said, “For buyers focused on affordability and range, the entry-level Uncharted Premium FWD model will be offered in limited numbers.”

Apparently, it wasn’t too limited. The 2027 Uncharted EV is now on sale, still with the base Premium FWD model equipped with a single 221-horsepower front-mounted electric motor.

Higher-priced Uncharted trims, including the Sport and GT, are upgraded with Subaru’s Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive system with X-Mode, delivering a combined 338 horsepower.

The 2027 Subaru Uncharted EV Premium FWD starts at $34,995, while the Sport and GT are priced from $39,795 and $43,795, respectively.

In the US, the 2027 Solterra and larger Trailseeker are still equipped with standard AWD, but Subaru is introducing new FWD (4×2) variants in some markets at a lower price point.

In comparison, the 2027 Subaru Solterra and Trailseeker EV start at $38,495 and $39,995, respectively.

Subaru opened preorders for its new 2027 electric range in Spain, including the Unchartered, Solterra, and E-Outback, which is sold as the Trailseeker in the US.

All of which will be available with a lower-priced FWD variant. Like the Uncharted, Subaru will still offer AWD on higher-priced Solterra and E-Outback trims.

The new Subaru Uncharted (4×2) starts at €26,525 ($28,900), the Solterra (4×2) starts at €35,025 ($38,200), and the E-Outback (4×2) starts at €36,525 ($39,800) in Spain, including subsidies, discounts, and other incentives.

Preorders are open for the Uncharted, while the Solterra and E-Outback are expected to launch in mid-2027.

Will Subaru expand FWD (4×2) to other vehicles and markets, like the US? The Uncharted is still Subaru’s only EV sold with standard FWD. The 2027 Solterra and Trailseeker are equipped with AWD and X-Mode.

For a small electric car driven on pavement I prefer RWD, which offers less complexity, better uphill traction, and a tighter turning circle. I love the handling of my last two cars, a RWD Miata and a RWD BMW i3 (old style).

Subaru is already selling considerably more EVs in the US, with three affordable, practical electric SUVs: the Uncharted, Solterra, and Trailseeker.

In Spring 2027, it will add its first three-row electric SUV, the Getaway. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see Subaru introduce a FWD option for other models, like the Solterra, at a lower price point.

Then again, AWD is used significantly more in the US than in Spain and other markets. For now, the Uncharted remains Subaru’s sole FWD model.

#4537. Hyundai’s new Kona N Line is already out testing [Video]

Hyundai isn’t just giving its compact SUV a fresh coat of paint. The next Kona is getting a major overhaul, and now we’ve caught an early glimpse of the N Line variant.

The Kona is getting an upgrade. Hyundai launched the second-generation Kona in 2023, so like most of its vehicles, a mid-cycle refresh is due around next year.

Apparently, that won’t be the case. Hyundai appears to be skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh for the third-generation Kona, with plans for a complete redesign.

Several disguised test vehicles have been spotted over the past few months in the US, Europe, and South Korea with a noticeably different design. The test mules sit higher off the ground and have a much more commanding, SUV-like shape, close to the new Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

Two versions have been captured thus far: a standard Kona and a more rugged XRT variant. For the first time, the new Kona N Line was spotted in Korea by HealerTV on a car carrier.

Since it’s still covered and an early-stage prototype, it’s hard to see many changes outside of the exclusive wheels and the added lower side skirt.

The new Kona N-Line is expected to receive other exclusive N Line design elements, including a more aggressive, sporty front and rear design with unique bumpers.

The early prototype sighting suggests Hyundai is keeping the N Line trim in the third-gen Kona lineup.

Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona Electric in the US but said it would return for the 2027 model year, when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

Like the current generation, the new Kona is expected to be available in gas, hybrid, and fully electric powertrains. It’s expected to debut in 2027 as a 2028 model year. Earlier this month, a prototype was captured in Korea that was expected to be the EV version (see the images here).

#4535. Planning to Stop Taking a GLP-1? Here’s How to Maintain Weight Loss

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Switching GLP-1 medications or undergoing bariatric surgery may help people maintain greater weight loss than stopping treatment entirely, according to a new study presented at ObesityWeek and published in eClinicalMedicine on November 14.

The Cleveland Clinic study compared five strategies for managing weight after treatment with GLP-1 medications, analyzing data from 20,486 adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes.

People who stop taking GLP-1 medications often regain weight. Researchers examined whether continuing treatment, switching medications, or undergoing bariatric surgery could help limit weight regain or support further weight loss.

The findings showed that people who underwent bariatric surgery or switched between semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Zepbound) experienced the greatest overall weight loss.

The study participants had an average age of 56.7 years, an average weight of 109 kg (240.3 lbs), and an average body mass index (BMI) of 38. All had been taking either semaglutide or tirzepatide for at least 90 days.

The researchers categorized the participants into five groups:

After 2 years, those who underwent bariatric surgery saw an average loss of 28.2% of their body weight or about 31.5 kg (69.4 lbs).

“We increasingly view medications and surgery as complementary tools rather than competing ones,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“For patients with severe obesity (typically a BMI of 35 or higher, or 30+ with metabolic conditions like type 2 diabetes), bariatric surgery remains the most durable, cost-effective intervention available,” he added. “Using a GLP-1 beforehand can safely reduce liver volume and lower surgical risk, while surgery provides the permanent anatomical and hormonal reset needed to maintain that weight loss long-term without relying indefinitely on weekly injections.”

During the same period, those who switched between semaglutide and tirzepatide lost 16% of their body weight, or about 18 kg (39.6 lbs).

Participants who switched from semaglutide to tirzepatide lost 3 kg (6.6 lbs) more than those who continued taking semaglutide. However, participants already taking tirzepatide lost 4.5 kg (9.9 lbs) more by continuing treatment rather than switching to semaglutide.

The other groups experienced lower amounts of weight loss:

After one year, participants with type 2 diabetes experienced HbA1c reductions of 1.76% following bariatric surgery, 1.43% after switching GLP-1 medications, and 1.32% after continuing their original medication, compared with 0.48% among those who discontinued treatment entirely.

After one year, participants with hypertension (high blood pressure) also experienced greater reductions in blood pressure following surgery or switching GLP-1 medications than those who discontinued treatment entirely.

“[This study] reinforces the need for a long term, multi-modal continuum of care rather than treating GLP-1s as a temporary fix,” said Ali.

Ali also recommended the following strategies to help maintain weight loss after stopping a GLP-1 medication:

The findings highlight the importance of having a long-term weight management plan in place before stopping a GLP-1 medication.

Before stopping a GLP-1 medication, talk with a healthcare professional. They can help you explore your options and determine which strategies may be most appropriate for your health needs.

Ali told Healthline that identifying the reason for stopping treatment is an important first step. He noted that people often discontinue GLP-1 medications because of gastrointestinal side effects, supply issues, or loss of insurance coverage rather than because they no longer need treatment.

He said that if side effects are the issue, adjusting the dose or switching to a different agent often solves the problem.

Ali also emphasized that stopping a GLP-1 medication shouldn’t be viewed as a test of willpower. Increased hunger after discontinuing treatment is a biological response, not a personal failure.

“Have a concrete ‘off-ramp’ plan in place with your doctor before taking your last dose, so you have medical, nutritional, or surgical support ready to protect the health gains you worked hard to achieve,” advised Ali.

#4534. F1 and Manufacturers Unanimously Agree to a Plan to Return to V8 Engines in 2030

The shrill roar of the V8 engines is set to return to the grid, with the FIA and F1 teams establishing the framework for a 2030 power-unit switch.

The FIA began the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend by announcing that all manufacturers have agreed to the framework to bring turbocharged V8 engines back to F1 and move away from the current V6 turbo.

This move has long been expected, with hopes that it will make engine building easier and cheaper while bringing back the sound that motorsport fans deeply miss.

The sound of the V8 engines was a rally cry for fans and has been sorely missed by audiences worldwide.

The F1 engine manufacturers agreed to a rough-out overarching plan to move to a 2.1-liter turbocharged V8 from 2030 onwards, with a lower charge of electrical power reducing the hybrid output from 350kW to 200kW, a decrease of nearly 56 percent.

The FIA announced that ‘The plan is to marry the V8 power unit to a chassis which will also be lighter, more agile and placing greater emphasis on driver skill and close racing.”

With everyone in agreement, PU manufacturers will start to jockey between improving the new car entering a sophomore season of new regulations and game planning for the major change coming just three seasons down the line.

It’s been 13 years since manufacturers last built a V8 engine for F1.

“This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1,” FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem said. “From the outset, I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

“The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this Championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide. Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.”

Victoria Beaver is a nomadic sports writer who spends her time hopping between race tracks and hippie farms. She’s covered every corner of motorsports that will let her in from 410 Sprints to NASCAR to Supercross. Her daily driver is a 2010 Subaru that she refused to do the smallest amount of preventative maintenance on. Instead, she spends her free time and money building a 42-foot Skoolie to one day travel the country full time.

#4533. Could a giant catapult launch someone to space? Short answer: Yes.

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 8:55 AM EST

For as long as humans have looked at the night sky, we’ve wondered what lies beyond Earth—and dreamed up ways of getting up there. These days, powerful rockets carrying tons of fuel are the tried-and-true method of escaping the planet’s gravitational pull and reaching space.

But what if, instead of modern rockets, we went medieval? Could a trebuchet or catapult—the massive siege weapons once used to fling stones at castles—launch a person into orbit? And if so, just how big would one have to be?

The answer requires a little imagination, a lot of physics, and a space-launching siege weapon of truly ridiculous proportions.

A catapult is essentially a giant lever used to hurl projectiles. Typically, they have a large, spoon-shaped throwing arm that’s wrenched back, creating tension, and then released, flinging an object over a great distance.

A trebuchet is a kind of catapult that uses a counterweight and gravity to launch projectiles. This machine’s long arm rests on a fulcrum, with a sling or cup for the projectile at one end and a heavy counterweight at the other.

When the arm is released, gravity pulls the counterweight downward, sending the opposite end—and its payload—soaring upward and forward.

Trebuchets are typically more powerful than catapults because they can launch heavier payloads over greater distances. So for our purposes, we’ll be focusing on a space trebuchet rather than a space catapult.

Trebuchets have been hurling heavy objects through the air for centuries. The structures are believed to have originated in China as early as the fifth century BC and eventually spread across Eurasia, becoming a formidable force in medieval warfare.

They arrived in Europe during the 12th century and quickly surpassed simple catapults.

Today, trebuchets are no longer used as weapons. But they remain popular as teaching tools for demonstrating physics principles—and for the decidedly more wholesome pursuit of seeing how far we can fling pumpkins, cabbages, and other projectiles.

So let’s crunch the numbers: Could a massive trebuchet really blast a human into orbit? Theoretically, yes. Practically, no.

For help answering this question, Popular Science turned to Frankie Zhu, an assistant professor in space robotics at the Colorado School of Mines in Golden, Colorado. Zhu gamely agreed to do some back-of-the-napkin math to put some numbers to this wildly improbable scenario.

“It just reminds me of a classic physics problem you would encounter in undergrad,” she says.

Before we can get to the heart of the calculations, Zhu says, we need to define some initial parameters. First, because the energy required to send a human into orbit depends on both mass and velocity, we need to know our imaginary astronaut’s mass. Zhu recommends 70 kilograms, or about 154 pounds.

Next, we need to define where space—and, for our purposes, orbit—begins. The conventional boundary is the Kármán line, an imaginary line 100 kilometers (about 62 miles) above sea level that is widely used to mark the edge of space. It’s the point at which Earth’s atmosphere becomes too thin for conventional aircraft to generate enough lift to stay aloft. “An orbit at 100 kilometers would be the lowest energy orbit possible,” she says.

To orbit Earth at the Kármán line—and not plummet back to the ground—a person needs to travel at approximately 7.85 kilometers per second, or 17,500 miles per hour, the same speed the International Space Station travels while orbiting Earth. “Any less and the human would fly up and then come back down in a parabolic trajectory,” she says.

If we assume that the atmosphere doesn’t produce drag on the human as they fly, then the velocity of the person leaving the trebuchet immediately after launch needs to be at least 7.97 kilometers per second, or 17,828 miles per hour. That extra bit of speed accounts for the energy needed to climb from Earth’s surface to the Kármán line.

To launch a human at that velocity, the trebuchet would need to store a massive amount of potential energy—about 2.22 billion joules, by Zhu’s calculations, similar to about 1,200 pounds of TNT. Zhu notes that she’s assuming 100 percent mechanical efficiency, meaning that none of the trebuchet’s stored energy is lost to friction, air resistance, sound, deformation, or the movement of the machine itself.

From here, we can move on to the design of the trebuchet. Based on Zhu’s math, the trebuchet would need a 5,000-ton counterweight—the equivalent of roughly 950 African bush elephants—which would need to drop at least 45.2 meters, or roughly 148 feet.

To turn the relatively slow movement of the massive counterweight into a hypersonic launch speed, the trebuchet would need an extreme mechanical leverage ratio of 379:1, she says. With these figures in mind, the trebuchet’s long throwing arm—the part with the human at the end of it—would need to be about 17.14 kilometers, or 10.7 miles, long.

“That should give you all the physical parameters of the trebuchet, ignoring some physics and human welfare,” she jokes.

How exactly would a human fare under these conditions? Fighter jet pilots can survive up to nine Gs using specialized G-suits, physical straining techniques, and intense centrifuge training. But, Zhu says, the “amount of Gs that the trebuchet is going to reach is…definitely past nine Gs. This human is not going to be alive when they make it to orbit.”

Another hurdle? Building the trebuchet. “To design a structure that can handle that amount of mass—the 5,000-ton counterweight—to support that mass and then to make something that large… that would be a humanity feat and a structural feat,” she says.

How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Why do we put seatbacks up for landing? An aviation expert explains.

A more human-friendly option, she says, might be a railgun, which uses electromagnetic forces to accelerate a projectile along a pair of conductive rails at extremely high speeds. To launch a person into orbit, a railgun would also need to be “really, really long,” she says. But because the human projectile could accelerate over a much greater distance and for a longer period of time, a railgun would theoretically offer a smoother acceleration profile—one that’s more amenable to human survival.

“Whereas [with] a trebuchet, the acceleration is going to be impulsive,” she says. “It’s going to be a huge smack at the very beginning if the structure doesn’t flex, if the structure is rigid.”

Rockets have been the standard for launching things into space since 1944, when Germany’s V-2 became the first human-made object to cross the Kármán line. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re the most efficient way to get there.

Rockets require enormous amounts of fuel, and all of that propellant has to be carried onboard. In other words, a rocket has to spend fuel lifting not just its payload, but also the fuel it needs to keep accelerating. This makes getting off Earth an inherently energy-intensive—and expensive—proposition.

With that in mind, engineers continue to explore other ways of getting into space, ideally using less fuel and resources. So far, though, most of their ideas haven’t made it off the drawing board—and, after crunching the numbers, Zhu says it’s highly unlikely that trebuchets will ever replace rockets.

“A lot of ideas are fantastical, some are possible, and an even smaller set are economical,” says Zhu.

#4532. The Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale Focuses On the Driver, Strips Out the Hybrid Parts

The lightest and most extreme 296 variant to date is not a particularly limited model, either.

The new-for-2026 Ferrari 296 Speciale is a sharper, faster, and more track-oriented variant of the brand’s V-6 supercar—but that doesn’t mean it is the only high-performance variant of the car that Ferrari will build. In a somewhat surprising break from recent tradition, Ferrari is also going to make a Challenge Stradale variant of the 296 to sell alongside the Speciale.

As the name suggests, the Challenge Stradale is a road-going variant of the 296 that shares a lot in common with the race car currently used in various Ferrari Challenge series. Specifically, its aerodynamic elements are strikingly similar to the new 296 Challenge Evo, which was revealed alongside the new road car on November 21. The massive rear wing, front dive planes, and aggressive rear splitter are all extremely similar to design elements seen on that race car.

Those components combine to create a massive 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour, an increase of 72 percent over the 296 GTB that won Road & Track Performance Car of the Year in 2024. Downforce is also up 401 lbs at that speed on the 296 Speciale, an increase of 29 percent.

The removal of the hybrid system means a reduction in power, dropping from a combined system output of 819 horsepower in the 296 GTB to an engine-only output of 670 hp in the Challenge Stradale. The simplified powertrain and stripped out interior mean serious reductions in weight to match, though; the Challenge Stradale is 309 lbs lighter than the GTB and 176 lbs lighter than the Speciale.

Does the reduction in weight and increase in downforce make the 296 Challenge Stradale faster than the hybrid 296 Speciale already on the market? Not necessarily. Ferrari claims the Challenge Stradale is half a second a lap faster at its Fiorano test track, but marginally slower at a high-speed circuit like Monza. The more powerful Speciale should be quicker on other tracks with the on-throttle time necessary to allow the hybrid to stretch its legs, while the lighter Challenge Stradale should have the advantage on more technical circuits with more off-throttle time.

The other major differentiation between the Speciale and the Challenge Stradale is availability. While that other high-end 296 variant was a limited-run model, Ferrari stresses that the Challenge Stradale is a part of its regular lineup, and should be more available to buyers. It remains a Ferrari, so the market is unlikely to be flooded with 296s with massive wings in the years to come, but by supercar standards, it should be relatively attainable.

Ferrari has not yet announced a price for the American market, but the brand says that it should start at the equivalent of just under $320,000 in Italy, including value-added tax. Prices in one region do not necessarily translate directly to another, but that number would leave the 296 Challenge Stradale in the general range of the similarly track-focused likes of Porsche’s 911 GT3 RS and Ford’s Mustang GTD.

#4531. Smart home gift guide: 40 clever gadgets to make any living space better using automation

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 9:45 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

The best smart home gift is the one that works the day it’s unwrapped, without a ladder, a landlord’s sign-off, or a surprise subscription. This guide covers every type of smart home dweller, from beginner to full-on Tony Stark. We started with easy plug-and-play options like a four-pack of Kasa Matter smart plugs and Philips Hue Essential bulbs that get up and running in minutes, along with new 2026 hardware we’ve tested hands-on, like Apple’s HomeView display. At the other end, upgrades like the Nest Learning Thermostat and the Emporia Vue 3 energy monitor reward a little more installation work.

Before you buy, find out which smart home platform your recipient already uses. Alexa, Google Home, and Apple Home still don’t share everything, though Matter-certified gear like the Eve Energy plug and the Govee Floor Lamp 2 works with all three. Some Matter devices connect over Thread, a low-power wireless network that needs a hub called a border router, such as a HomePod mini 2 or a Google TV Streamer, to reach the rest of the house. The entries flag the hubs, extra hardware, and monthly plans that can turn a gift into homework. Prices come from makers and major retailers and were checked in November 2026, so expect them to move during holiday sales.

If you’re shopping for a cook, the smart ovens and smokers are in our kitchen gift guide. If you’re building out a whole system rather than shopping for one gift, start with our guide to the best smart home devices.

Amazon kept the old shape and changed the guts inside. The sixth-generation Echo Dot adds a built-in smart home hub for Zigbee, Matter, and Thread gear, so it can pair devices on its own instead of leaning on a separate bridge. Amazon also claims 50 percent more bass than the model it replaces, though anyone buying primarily for music should watch for holiday discounts or spend $20 more on the Echo Dot Max. Its built-in eero extender stretches Wi-Fi by up to 1,000 square feet in houses that already run eero, and Alexa+ is included with Prime or costs $19.99 a month without it.

An all-in-one gift for backyard birdwatchers, the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro pairs 4K HDR with PDAF Auto Focus for sharp close-ups, plus 1080p/120 fps slow motion for fleeting moments. FeatherPal AI identifies more than 10,000 species with an eligible subscription, while the 5W solar roof and removable hopper simplify upkeep. Now $199.99—save $60 at its lowest price of the year through December 27.

Google went six years without a new smart speaker before the Google Home Speaker arrived in June. Built around Gemini for Home, it includes a Thread border router and handles everyday jobs like switching lights and adjusting a thermostat without a subscription. Gemini Live conversations and extra AI features require Google Home Premium, which starts at $10 a month. Buy it for someone who already runs their house from the Google Home app.

The hub that makes Apple Home work away from home

For a household built around iPhones, the HomePod mini 2 is the speaker that lets Apple’s Home app run automations and control gear from away. It runs on an S10 chip with Wi-Fi 6E and Thread, acting as a hub for HomeKit and Matter accessories. Buy it for that hub job first: Apple says Siri’s bigger AI upgrades arrive in a future software update, and the personal features need an iPhone or iPad that supports Apple Intelligence. An Apple TV 4K handles the same hub duties for anyone who would rather have a streaming box.

Apple’s first smart display doubles as a home hub

Apple’s first smart display, HomeView, puts a 7-inch touchscreen on the kitchen counter for music, FaceTime calls, and Apple Home controls, while serving as a home hub alongside the HomePod mini 2. In our hands-on review, we found it very helpful, if a little quirky.

It recognizes up to six people by face and surfaces their own messages, calendars, and reminders, though only when that person’s paired iPhone or iPad is nearby and recently unlocked. Stick to the tabletop model as a gift: the wall-mounted version starts at the same $299, but it requires a separate Schneider Home wall mount starting at $59.95 (plus a user-supplied 20-watt USB-C power adapter for the base mount).

Philips Hue used to be the smart bulb you bought only after getting serious about smart home tech. The Hue Essential line changes the math with an affordable four-pack of color bulbs that connect over Bluetooth and work from the Hue app without a bridge. Each bulb puts out 800 lumens and dims down to 2 percent. Adding them to Alexa, Google Home, or Apple Home runs through Matter and takes a compatible hub, such as an Echo, a Nest Hub, or a HomePod mini 2, and they can always move onto a Hue Bridge later.

Two color bulbs that work with every major platform

A pair of GE Cync Full Color bulbs is a low-stakes way to test smart lighting on two bedside lamps. They connect straight to 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi in the Cync app with no hub, and Matter support brings them into Alexa, Google Home, Apple Home, and SmartThings when paired with a compatible Matter hub. Each puts out 800 lumens, matching the Hue Essential bulbs above, and if the recipient hates smart home gear, they still work like regular bulbs.

Four plugs that work with every major assistant

This four-pack of Kasa Matter smart plugs is the easiest way to automate something your recipient already owns, whether that’s a lamp, a holiday tree, or a coffee maker. Each slim plug leaves the second wall outlet free, handles up to 15 amps, tracks energy use, and connects to Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home through Matter. Just note that they only join a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network.

Buy Eve Energy for someone who doesn’t want a living-room lamp checking in with a company server. Eve says it needs no cloud account or registration, and it communicates locally over Matter and Thread while tracking power draw. Because it relies on Thread, the house needs a border router like a HomePod mini 2 or a Google TV Streamer. At $39.95, you’re paying nearly as much for one plug as you would for the Kasa four-pack above.

The GE Cync Outdoor Smart Plug puts holiday lights and porch string lights on two independently controlled outlets rated for wet locations, with covers for both sockets and a 15-amp ceiling. This model connects to Alexa and Google Assistant straight over Wi-Fi. Its Amazon listing doesn’t mention Apple Home, so iPhone households should look for GE’s newer Matter-compatible version instead.

Four outlets that work with Apple Home too

Competition for outlets is fierce behind my desk and TV. It’s probably like that for you, too. The Meross Smart Power Strip has four outlets that switch independently, so the TV, the game console and the lamp behind them can each follow a different schedule. Its four USB ports switch as a group, and surge protection is built in. It connects over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi with no hub and works with Apple Home, Alexa, Google Home and SmartThings, though controlling it through Apple Home from outside the house takes a home hub like a HomePod mini 2.

Color accent lighting for Apple, Google and Alexa homes

Despite what an electrician will tell you, it’s possible to revamp a room’s lighting without breaking into the wiring. The Govee Floor Lamp 2 is rated for up to 1,725 lumens, with independent lighting for the pole and base. Matter support drops it straight into Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, or SmartThings without a Govee-only workaround, though it ships in pieces, so plan on a few minutes of assembly.

Christmas lights that know the shape of the tree

Unlike standard app-controlled holiday lights that just change color, Twinkly Strings use a phone’s camera to map where every bulb sits on the tree, then animate patterns across that exact shape. This 100-LED Gen II strand connects over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth and can’t be cut to length. Twinkly says you can sync up to 4,000 LEDs across multiple sets, which helps, since 100 bulbs won’t cover a full-size tree on their own.

Give the Hatch Restore 3 to anyone who dreads a phone alarm blaring six inches from their face. It brightens gradually like a sunrise in the morning and handles wind-down lighting and sound at night. Sunrise alarms, wind-down lights, and a basic sound library all work without a subscription, while the optional Hatch+ sleep library runs $5.99 a month or $59.99 a year after a 30-day free trial.

Family members add photos and videos to the Aura Carver from Aura’s app, so new pictures keep showing up long after the holidays, with no subscription and no storage limit. The 10.1-inch landscape screen pairs two portrait shots side by side so they fill the display. You can preload photos before it ships so it comes out of the box ready to go. Just double-check which album you pick before Grandma gets an unexpected slideshow.

Sized for a bedroom, controlled from a phone

This gift doesn’t have to be passive-aggressive, but it can be. Levoit recommends the Core 300S-P for bedrooms and offices up to 219 square feet, since the 1,058-square-foot figure in its listings assumes only one air change an hour. It connects to the free VeSync app for remote control, responds to Alexa and Google Assistant, and ships with a three-stage filter already installed alongside an indicator that flags when it needs replacing.

Answers the question of whether the cat ate

The Petlibro Granary Smart Camera Feeder answers the question every pet owner texts the sitter: Did the cat eat? It holds 5 liters of kibble, connects over 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz Wi-Fi, and schedules dry-food meals from an app while watching the bowl with a 1080p, 145-degree night-vision camera and two-way audio. Petlibro’s Video Cloud plans start at $59.99 a year for seven days of storage, or clips can be saved locally to a microSD card (sold separately).

Think of the Google TV Streamer as an entertaining Trojan horse for sneaking a smart hub into the living room. Beyond 4K HDR with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, it doubles as a Matter hub and Thread border router, anchoring gear like the Eve Energy plug and putting a home control panel right on the TV. Google doesn’t include an HDMI cable, so tuck one into the gift bag.

Person and pet alerts without a monthly bill

Unwrapping a gadget that immediately hands you a monthly bill is a terrible gift experience, which is why the Tapo C120 keeps its subscription optional. It distinguishes people, pets, and vehicles without a paid plan and saves footage to a microSD card up to 512 GB (not included). You get 2K QHD video, color night vision from dual spotlights, Alexa and Google Assistant support, and an IP66 rating for outdoor use wherever an outlet is in reach of its power cord. Tapo Care cloud storage is there only if you want it.

For a front door without existing wiring, the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K (2nd gen) runs on a built-in rechargeable battery and records Retinal 2K video with 6× zoom. Ring’s $49.99 Solar Charger keeps it topped up for anyone who doesn’t want to pull it off the frame to recharge. Saving and reviewing clips does require a Ring subscription, with Ring Solo covering one device for $4.99 a month.

A smart lock that keeps the landlord’s key working

Because the SwitchBot Lock Ultra mounts over the inside thumbturn of an existing deadbolt, renters get smart access without replacing the cylinder or cutting off the landlord’s key.

This Vision Combo bundles a keypad that unlocks with 3D facial recognition alongside a Hub Mini for remote control and Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home support. Some deadbolt shapes need a separate $20 adapter kit, so take a quick look at the door before you wrap it.

Sticking a SwitchBot Bot next to a coffee maker or air conditioner gives an old appliance a tiny robotic finger to push its button on command. It sticks next to a rocker switch or push button with an adhesive pad. Out of the box, it runs over Bluetooth in the SwitchBot app; remote access and voice commands through Alexa, Google Assistant, or Siri require a separate SwitchBot hub.

The battery-powered Hue Dimmer Switch puts a real button back on the wall for houseguests, mounting with adhesive or screws and lifting off its magnetic plate to work from the couch. It dims Hue lights and cycles through scenes, and Hue’s setup guide says it can pair directly with up to 10 bulbs. App customization and routines still require a Hue Bridge, so it makes the most sense for someone who already owns one.

Stick the Aqara Door and Window Sensor P2 on a door or window, and opening it can switch on a hall light or fire off a phone alert. It runs on a CR123A battery and joins Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, or SmartThings over Matter and Thread. Make sure the recipient already has a Thread border router like the HomePod mini 2 or Google TV Streamer, because the sensor won’t work without one.

Three sensors for the spots that flood first

A leak sensor may seem like a boring gift until you consider the pain of a water heater disaster. This GoveeLife Water Leak Detector 1s kit bundles three IP67-rated sensors and a Wi-Fi gateway that sends a phone alert when one of them gets wet, while each puck sounds a 105-decibel alarm. Govee claims five years of battery life. Tuck them under the water heater, the washing machine, and the kitchen sink.

The Rachio Smart Hose Timer threads onto an outdoor faucet, runs schedules from Rachio’s app, and skips a watering when rain is in the forecast. The starter kit includes one valve and the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi hub it requires, and a single hub can manage up to eight valves. Grab a pair of AA batteries (not included), and in cold climates remind the recipient it’s a gift for spring that needs to come indoors before a hard freeze.

Solar power, two lenses and no monthly bill

Mounted outdoor cameras are a pain to pull down for charging, so the eufy SoloCam S340 brings its own solar panel, which eufy says stays topped up on two hours of direct sun a day. It pairs a 3K wide-angle lens and a 2K telephoto lens for 8× hybrid zoom, pans 344 degrees, saves clips to 8 GB of built-in storage with no monthly fee, and works with Alexa and Google Assistant. At full MSRP, it sits just $10 under eufy’s newer SoloCam E50 ($229.99), so watch for holiday discounts on the S340 or check which model the listing shows.

The alarm Google sells now that the Nest Protect is gone

Google stopped making the Nest Protect, and the First Alert SC5 is the smart alarm the Google Store sells in its place. It detects smoke and carbon monoxide, sends phone alerts, and can be checked, silenced, or tested from the First Alert or Google Home apps. It even interconnects with existing Nest Protects so every unit sounds together, making it a timely drop-in swap as older Nest Protects reach their expiration dates after about 10 years. This battery model needs no wiring, though homes with hardwired alarms should opt for First Alert’s hardwired version instead.

Comes with a sensor for the room that’s always too hot

Our utility bills went haywire last year, and that makes the math on a smart thermostat much more attractive. Google’s fourth-generation Nest Learning Thermostat includes a Nest Temperature Sensor for the room that never feels right, is designed to work in most homes without a common power wire (C-wire), and supports Matter so it also shows up in Apple Home. It’s sold only in the U.S. and Canada.

The ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium packs a lot onto one wall plate: radar occupancy detection, an indoor air quality monitor, and a built-in Alexa speaker, plus a remote SmartSensor in the box. Siri works on it too in homes that already have a HomePod or HomePod mini 2. The company claims it can cut heating and cooling costs by up to 26 percent, or as much as $284 a year, and fit more than 95 percent of HVAC systems.

Unlocks with a tap of an iPhone or Apple Watch

The Schlage Encode Plus is the deadbolt to buy for iPhone households, unlocking with a tap of an iPhone or Apple Watch via Apple Home Keys while also supporting Alexa and Google Assistant. Built-in Wi-Fi means no separate bridge for the Schlage app, Alexa, or Google, though remote Apple Home control takes a home hub like a HomePod mini 2 or Apple TV.

Schlage’s app manages up to 100 access codes for guests and dog walkers, and a physical backup key comes in the box. Schlage estimates four AA batteries last up to six months with typical use. Because it replaces the whole deadbolt, confirm the recipient is allowed to swap theirs before wrapping it.

Smart lights that survive someone flipping the switch

Put the Lutron Diva smart dimmer on your list for anyone tired of guests killing smart bulbs at the wall. It replaces the switch with a familiar paddle, and this starter kit bundles Lutron’s Caséta hub and a Pico remote to tie the lights into Alexa, Apple Home, Google Home, Ring, and Sonos. Better yet, it handles up to 150 watts of LEDs without needing a neutral wire (the extra return wire missing from many older switch boxes).

The Meross MSG100HK puts an end to circling back down the street to check whether the garage door closed. It wires into an existing opener instead of replacing the motor, requires no subscription, and covers Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Assistant. Run the opener through Meross’s compatibility checker first, since Chamberlain, LiftMaster, and Craftsman units may need a separate accessory that Meross ships at no charge.

Skips the watering when it already rained

Rachio has sold the Rachio 3 for years, and it’s still the company’s main sprinkler controller. It replaces the timer on an existing in-ground irrigation system, installs in 30 minutes or less according to Rachio, and runs on a free app with weather skips that hold off on watering after rain. A 16-zone version costs $249.99, and the controller pairs with the Tempest weather station further down this list.

Find out which circuit is eating the electric bill

The Emporia Vue 3 shows which circuits are eating the electric bill, though it can’t separate two appliances that share a circuit. The kit includes two main sensors and 16 branch sensors, and the company claims customers save an average of 10 percent on their bills.

Those sensors clamp onto wires inside the breaker panel, so plan on an electrician unless the recipient is qualified to work in one.

For anyone who wonders what’s floating around their house, with or without a basement, the Airthings View Plus tracks odorless radon alongside fine dust (PM2.5), carbon dioxide, chemical fumes (VOCs), humidity, temperature, and air pressure with no subscription. Airthings says it runs up to two years on six AA batteries, or it can stay plugged in over USB-C.

The Eureka E20 Evo Plus docks at a bagless self-emptying station, so there are no replacement bags to reorder. It’s rated for 10,000 Pa of suction and maps rooms with lidar. Eureka says the station’s 2-liter bin needs emptying every couple of weeks in a typical home, though the trade-off is dumping that dusty bin into the trash by hand.

A backyard weather station with no moving parts

Turn a backyard into a personal weather lab with the Tempest Weather Station. It uses zero moving parts, measuring wind with ultrasonic sensors and rain with a haptic sensor, and feeds those readings into its own local forecasts with no subscription. The 2026 revision adds bigger solar panels and a replaceable battery.

It integrates with Alexa, Siri, IFTTT, and Rachio, so a rainy morning can cancel the sprinklers automatically. A flat base and pole mount come in the box, but supplying the actual fence post or mast in an open spot is up to the buyer.

Turns existing Hue bulbs into motion sensors

Anyone with a pile of Hue bulbs will get more out of a Hue Bridge Pro than another lamp. It supports more than 150 lights, and Philips says it responds five times faster than the standard bridge. Its MotionAware feature turns groups of three or four compatible Hue bulbs into motion sensors that switch lights on automatically, though security motion alerts and alarms require a paid plan.

One interface for a house full of gadgets

For the person who already owns half of this list, the next gift is a single interface to wrangle it all. Home Assistant Green arrives with the open-source Home Assistant software preinstalled, plugs into a router over Ethernet, and packs 4 GB of RAM and 32 GB of storage. Zigbee gear requires a separate Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2 adapter.

The software is free and runs locally inside the house. Reaching it remotely, or linking it to Alexa or Google Assistant, takes either networking know-how or Nabu Casa’s optional Home Assistant Link subscription ($6.50 a month or $65 a year). Nabu Casa raised the box’s suggested price to $199 this year, citing memory costs.

#4530. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: Why One Big Meal Isn’t the Real Holiday Health Problem

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In the classic Thanksgiving comedy Planes, Trains and Automobiles, hapless hero Del Griffith (played by the late, great John Candy) delivers an emotional riposte to Steve Martin’s uptight ad man Neal Page that stands as a beautifully dignified defense of kindness, empathy and self-love in the face of his own perceived shortcomings.

“You want to hurt me? Go right ahead if it makes you feel any better…I could be a cold, hard cynic like you. But I don’t like to hurt people’s feelings. You think what you want about me, I’m not changing. I… I like me. My wife likes me…because I’m the real article. What you see is what you get.”

For many of us around the holidays, particularly after a night of excess, Del and Neal’s exchange could read as our internal monologue – your kinder inner voice battling the internal bully who judges your every overindulgence. The jury’s out on whether the kind voice is ever as potent as Del’s is in that moment. But it should be, because when it comes to your health around the holidays, the bully has usually got it wrong.

The truth is, for most of us, one day of immoderation during Thanksgiving is unlikely to matter in the grand scheme. As such, you would do well to avoid the litany of holiday season health myths out there, many of which seem hell-bent on punishing you for taking a day off:

Like all misinformation, these kinds of medical myths are loud and tend to die hard, but they almost always trade on quick fixes that target the wrong thing.

A 2020 review of 23 observational studies found that most showed significant weight gain during festive periods, averaging roughly a pound and a half. One of the original studies, a landmark NIH study from 2000, found that much of that weight tends to stick around. So the question is not what you ate on Thanksgiving Thursday and how quickly you can “undo the damage,” but rather whether the extended holiday season becomes a two-month period where your healthy routine goes out the window. Some things to look out for on that front:

None of this is a free pass for everyone. If you manage a health condition, you likely have less margin for error, even when talking about a single meal or a drink. Critical factors include timing, sodium intake, alcohol intake, and missed medication. A few non-exhaustive examples:

Whatever condition you’re managing, the move for all of them remains the same – be prepared. Check your plan with your care team before the holiday, not after, and call them if something feels off afterward.

Technically, feeling good on Black Friday starts on Thursday. A short and light walk after a feast can help smooth out post-meal blood sugar – the earlier the better, ideally within an hour of eating. Staying upright for a couple of hours to help with digestion, particularly if you’re prone to reflux, is also a great idea. If you’re on medication, remember to take it on time. And, at the risk of sounding prudish, and this goes for everyone: try to get to bed at a sensible hour.

Above all else, Thanksgiving is a holiday built around gratitude and kindness, so channel your inner Del Griffith and remember to be both grateful and kind, to yourself and to those around you – evidence suggests that’s also good for your health.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4529. Las Vegas Grand Prix Delivers 50 Laps of Close Battles While Verstappen Holds On to Win

Verstappen won in Vegas for the third time in four years, but with 35 lead changes and 352 overtakes, the Las Vegas Grand Prix was far from ordinary.

Max Verstappen started on pole for the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Saturday evening and held the lead at one point on every lap, but the race was far more thrilling than that would let on.

Verstappen qualified second and inherited pole after pole-sitter Kimi Antonelli received a five-place grid penalty.

At the start, Max Verstappen took the lead from George Russell and kept his elbows out as he had the hardest spot on the track, punching through the crisp air with no help from a slipstream.

On the second lap of the race, Russell, in a much faster Mercedes, passed Verstappen in the final corners coming off the Las Vegas Strip straight, then lost the lead before the first corner of the next lap. He would repeat this multiple times throughout the first half of the Grand Prix.

The race recorded a record 35 lead changes, but no one could cement a run past Verstappen.

With Verstappen slowing the field behind him, the first 10 laps of the race found the top three within one second and the top ten within less than 4.5 seconds.

On lap 20, Sergio Perez tried to make a pick on Rafeal Camera and the Haas, and Cadillac ended up tangled in the barrier, bringing out a full safety car. In a normal race, this would’ve neutralized the race, but with everyone still running bunched up, it just sent the field all together to the pits, leading to teams double-stacking against each other.

Hamilton was the biggest loser at the pit stop, having to serve a 10-second penalty that was not yet shared with him for a battle with Norris that he thought was just.

Hamilton was kept out while everyone else pitted to clear space for Charles Leclerc and was told about his penalty.

“Ah, that’s shit. If I turned in, we would’ve crashed.”

Under the safety car, Arvid Lindblad spun on cold tires to end his campaign for his first-ever podium. Arvid had his best starting spot of fifth for the Grand Prix and ran as high as third, while the Red Bulls on his sister team ran 1-2; he fell out of the points with the mistake.

Shortly after racing resumed, Isack Hadjar, who challenged his teammate Verstappen for the lead in the first half of the race and often put in the hardest position between the leader and the charging field, hit debris on the track and damaged his front wing. Hadjar pitted and finished outside the points as well.

With Red Bull and VCARB drivers out of contention, the door reopened for the Mercedes as Kimi Antonelli made his way into the picture following his grid drop, and Russell never left.

With two laps to go, Antonelli led Russell as the teammate fought for second; in turn 5, Russell went for the pass, overcommitted, and slid into the barrier.

Verstappen laughed on from ahead following a weekend of tension between the front-row starters.

Antonelli fell away from the lead battle on the penultimate lap with an internal issue and would come home fourth.

In the mayhem, the McLarens saw their luck change at Las Vegas. Following this double disqualification while battling for the championship last year, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri walked away with a shocking first double podium of the season.

“I led for about 15 seconds, so I’m very proud,” Norris joked.

Antonelli was followed by Pierre Gasly, Franco Colapinto, Lewis Hamilton, Carlos Sainz, George Russell and Charles Leclerc in the points-paying positions.

#4528. One of the world’s biggest zinc mines is getting Alaska’s largest solar farm

Red Dog Mine in Alaska burns about 40,000 gallons of diesel a day to keep one of the world’s largest zinc mines running, and now, an 8.8-megawatt (MW) solar farm and battery storage will help cut that fuel use.

The Alaska Energy Authority’s board unanimously approved a nearly $5 million loan for the project through its Power Project Fund. Tugliq Red Dog1 will build, own, and operate the roughly $35 million solar project and sell the electricity to mine operator Teck Alaska. The state’s loan review says site work began in June and expects the solar and storage to come online in October 2028.

Red Dog sits about 105 miles north of the Arctic Circle, on land owned by NANA, an Iñupiat-owned Alaska Native corporation. The array would be larger than any solar farm operating in Alaska today, as KOTZ’s Desiree Hagen reported for Alaska Public Media. Hagen reported that the plans call for more than 15,000 panels across around 30 acres.

The mine gets all its power from on-site diesel generators. In summer, it can draw so much electricity that Teck has to cut power elsewhere at the site. The solar array and the 8.8 MW, 15 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery will give the operator another source of power during those crunches.

The state of Alaska expects the solar and storage project to cover about 5% of the zinc mine’s electricity needs under its current operating plan. The project could do even more after mining ends, covering about 90% of the site’s annual electricity needs.

Cost to import sun to a remote Alaskan village 0, cost to import diesel quite high.

A 500W panel weighs 60 lbs about the same as 9 gallons of diesel. 500W panel generates 750kwh of electricity a year each and every year for 20 years. 9 gallons of diesel gives you 350kwh of thermal energy which yields varying amounts of desired output.

Teck expects the mine’s existing deposits to support operations through 2031, and it’s studying whether to develop two nearby deposits. If that expansion goes ahead, the state projects the solar and battery project would cover about 3% of the larger operation’s electricity needs. If mining ends, demand will drop sharply, but the site will still need electricity for cleanup and long-term water treatment.
