#4386. Tested: 2027 Audi SQ7 Is the Punchier 3-Row SUV

Audi's twin-turbo V-8 makes plenty of the right noises, and a deft chassis makes it fun on a twisting road as well.

Audi is slicing its bread thin when it comes to three-row performance SUVs. Below the flagship SQ9, there’s now a 2027 Audi SQ7. It’s the SQ9’s doppelgänger, minus a few inches of length and wearing what will be a more familiar badge for longtime Audi buyers. This is the third generation of Q7 and, like before, it straddles the space between a BMW X5 and X7, or a Mercedes-Benz GLE and GLS. And thankfully, the S model marches on with a bruiser of a V-8 engine. Audi pitched it as the SUV for the “performance family,” which is a concept that may have lost a little in translation. No matter the 0–60 of your family, though, this SQ7 is more than adept at moving lots of people around in a fast, fun manner.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Every SQ7 comes with Audi’s familiar 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 under the hood, and this version makes 90 hp more than the outgoing model. The numbers come in at 590 hp and 591 lb-ft of torque, sent through the same new, rear-biased Quattro all-whee- drive system that debuted on the SQ9. Shifting is handled by a ZF eight-speed automatic transmission, and Audi claims a 3.7-second 0–60-mph time, one-tenth quicker than the bigger SQ9. When equipped with optional summer rubber, the SQ7 tops out at a limited 155 mph.

Transmission: Eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

EPA MPG: 15/20/17 mpg (city/highway/combined)

The TL;DR summary? Refer to my Audi SQ9 review from last month. The dynamic experience of both cars is overwhelmingly similar. But there are some small but significant differences which are worth exploring in more depth.

Like the SQ9, the SQ7 offers an optional Sport adaptive air suspension that lowers the ride height by 0.6 inch, fits more aggressive anti-roll bars, and tweaks the tune of the adaptive dampers and air suspension. While the SQ9 I drove was not fitted with this suspension, the SQ7 I tested was.

As advertised, this optional suspension is indeed more dynamic than the standard setup. The big SUV went from, sure, you can drive it hard if you want, to, this thing is actually kind of fun. Of course, the 5.5-inch shorter wheelbase, a near-nine-inch reduction in overall length, and the 100-pound diet compared to the SQ9 does some heavy lifting here too. On the Sport setup, the SQ7 turned in more quickly and benefited from notably improved body control. Plus, power distribution is clearly more pronounced from the back axle than it is in the standard Q7 on account of the heavily rear-biased Quattro system shared with the SQ9. It’s still not as rigid or as hardcore as an X7 M60 or an AMG GLE 63 S, but Audi is moving in that direction with its sportier tune.

The SQ7 makes its V-8 soundtrack known to a slightly more obvious degree than the SQ9 too. This could be down to my slightly closer proximity to the quad-tipped exhaust from the driver’s seat, or minor improvements in sound deadening, but whatever the reason, it’s improved. The V-8 rumble and meaty rip to its 7000-rpm redline were like a luxurious dessert I never tired of taking bites out of. The new SQ7’s raw pace is improved over the outgoing model, with the extra 90 horses over the previous SQ7 obvious whenever I pushed.

Fuel economy is the big loser here. I looked down after 100 miles of California canyon road driving and noticed the trip computer readout stating 11.4 mpg. More typical driving will be better at 17 mpg combined, per the EPA rating, but expect this big SUV to gulp down the premium stuff.

There’s little to no penalty in ride when you spec the firmer suspension. The difference is so minute that it took some deep concentration over similar stretches of road to discern any penalty to comfort versus the regular Q7. If anything, there’s a touch of additional flintiness to the biggest impacts, which could just as easily be the fault of the 23-inch wheels and summer tires fitted to the SQ7 compared to the 22-inch all-seasons on the Q7. Whatever the reduction in comfort may be, the drop in ride height is worth it purely from an appearance perspective. With the Midnight Green Metallic–painted body (I know, it looks black) hugging the black-painted multi-spoke wheels, the SQ7 would make for a perfect villain car in a spy thriller.

Here’s where you really need to make the tough decision between SQ7 and SQ9. Are you planning on using the third row frequently? If so, don’t pass go, head directly to the 9. If you’re just in the game for a larger SUV and might use the third row on occasion, then the SQ7 is the one to get. The big difference isn’t necessarily in the amount of space for third-row passengers, but in cargo room with the third row in place.

Surprisingly, legroom in the wayback is identical between the two. But clambering into said space was much tougher in the SQ7 thanks to a narrower crawl-through gap behind the second row (available with a standard bench or optional captain’s chairs). Once situated, life is pretty much the same in both three-row Audis. The 4.2 cubic feet of reduced cargo space in the SQ7 will make it so that you won’t be able to bring as many goodies to the picnic as an SQ9 can carry, though.

From a driver’s perspective, the SQ7’s cabin is about as good as it gets in a modern Audi. The whole layout, from the screens to the center console and feature set, is identical to the SQ9 flagship, so you could consider this a junior flagship. Optional auto-opening and -closing doors can be had. The Digital Matrix LED headlights that are so astoundingly cool in the SQ9 come standard here. Bang & Olufsen 4-D sound (also optional) with exciters in the seats makes for one hell of an audio experience.

And if you like screens, Audi’s got ’em. The 11.9-inch digital cluster blends into the 14.5-inch central infotainment system, and the 12.3-inch passenger display comes standard. I wish there were more physical controls, especially for the frustrating screen-controlled air vents, but at least Audi supplies some buttons and knobs both on the steering wheel and center console.

Luxury accoutrements by way of unexpected or interesting material usage are plentiful. The carbon-weave trim stands out versus traditional glossy carbon fiber. Funky fabrics on the doors and contrast stitching are appropriately nice touches. Audi claims it’s trying to do better with how it presents its interiors by doing away with piano-black plastic, and while this effort is a good start, there’s still plenty to go around on the dash, steering wheel, and center console.

The approximately $19,000 you’ll save on the SQ7 over the SQ9 sure is a motivating factor for picking the smaller three-row. Its slightly better driving dynamics are another good one, but again, it’s all about priorities here. An extra-large family would be better served by the larger option.

For now, BMW doesn’t offer an X5 M60 with a V-8, and the AMG price match is the inline-six PHEV GLE 53. In other words, this gas-powered V-8 performance SUV has a little niche of its own for the time being. A Porsche Cayenne S is considerably more expensive to start, and the gap only widens when the option book comes into play.

There’s a lot going for this latest generation of Audi’s smaller three-row, and outside of some small digital quirks you need to get over, it talks a persuasive game. Audi nailed the powertrain with this V-8 and its rear-biased Quattro system. And despite the SQ7’s sporty potential, there’s little compromise when it comes to usability here. The styling is arguably a bit soft in spots, but it has far more attitude than the brand’s electric offerings thanks to an upright face and pronounced fender flares.

The rear-wheel steering does an excellent job of making the SQ7 drive smaller than it should. It comes standard and can turn the rear wheels up to five degrees in the opposite direction to tighten the turning radius or make the SUV dive into corners with the eagerness you’d expect from a much smaller vehicle. This, combined with lighter-than-typical and progressive steering from Audi, removed that sensation of excessive size from the driver’s seat.

#4385. BYD Just Put a Fold-Away Steering Wheel in a Car People Can Buy

One touch of a button and you instantly get extra cabin space to relax.

Anyone who has ever tried to eat lunch sitting in the driver’s seat while parked—or worse yet, flip open a laptop to catch up on emails—knows that a steering wheel takes up a surprisingly large amount of real estate. Thus, manufacturers of all kinds have come up with various steering solutions that have largely remained conceptual, cool show-off pieces for the auto show circuit but little more. Chinese manufacturer BYD just stuck one in a mainstream SUV.

The Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 is a large six-seater SUV that’s about the size of an Infiniti QX80, with prices starting at the equivalent of $41K in the Chinese market. It’s not a pure EV, but rather a series plug-in hybrid with a 150-hp 1.5-liter turbo four-cylinder acting as a generator to power the 66-kWh battery pack; the dual electric motors combine for 536 hp.Fang Cheng Bao is one of BYD’s subbrands, aimed at delivering an off-road-ready flair. The Tai 9 is certainly a chunky-looking thing, but what’s perhaps most interesting about the top trim level is how it behaves when parked.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147

Spend the equivalent of $49K for the highest-grade Tai 9, and you get a folding steering wheel that disappears into the dash. Because the vehicle is entirely steer-by-wire, a technology that only became legal in China less than six months ago, the Tai 9 has no steering column geometry to worry about. The rim splits in half, folds back over the column, and the whole thing retracts, airbag still facing forward.Paired with a driver’s seat that reclines almost completely flat, the appeal here is to provide a more spacious place to relax or work while you charge. Again, this feature is only available when parked, so you can’t retract the wheel while using the Tai 9’s driver-assistance functions.

However, this folding steering wheel does show how car interiors might look for vehicles with Level 4-or-higher autonomy, ones that can operate completely without human intervention in certain cases. On a geofenced section of highway, with automated cruise control activated, you could simply pack your steering wheel away for extra room.

Obviously, driving enthusiasts who obsess over steering feel aren’t going to be too happy about the proliferation of steering-by-wire, never mind having the steering wheel fold away entirely. However, it’s not like a three-ton, three-row PHEV SUV is going to feel like piloting a Caterham anyway.

What’s perhaps most impressive of all is the speed at which BYD managed to get its folding steering wheel technology into the hands of the public, considering the regulatory requirements only came into being months ago. Combined with the company’s production-car speed record under its Yangwang performance brand, and the sub-$10K price of its Seagull entry-level EV, BYD is certainly active in all segments of the market. Watch this space to see what it gets up to next.

#4383. Europe Gets This Tiny New Suzuki EV. It Makes A Mini Look Big

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Suzuki left the U.S. car market in 2012, but it still builds the kind of small hatchbacks European buyers have long favored, now also powered by electricity. Its latest is the Ignis EV, a city car that measures just 11 feet 9 inches long (3.57 meters). It’s due in Europe in summer 2027, when it will face a new generation of small EVs from both European and Chinese automakers.

The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan. The company recently launched the e Sky there, an electric kei car that supplies the basis for the Ignis’s body and powertrain. The Ignis still has the typical kei proportions (it's tall and narrow), but Suzuki says it took the car onto European city streets and winding roads to tune the suspension and power delivery, making it more appealing to the people it hopes will buy one.

A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform. Yes, that really is what it's called. Up front, the motor, inverter, and reduction gears share a single compact assembly that sends 90 horsepower and 98 pound-feet (133 Nm) to the front wheels. Suzuki says it chose LFP for safety and longevity, but it hasn’t given the European car a range or charging figure yet.

The Ignis EV has a very tight 29.5-foot (9-meter) turning circle. Its overhangs are tiny, giving it a wheel-at-each-corner stance that looks unique while maximizing available interior room. The LED signatures at both ends take their shape from digital numerals, and the dark pillars give the roof a floating look.

Inside, a curve runs from the dashboard into the doors, with a wide display and a ceramic-inspired storage tray across the dash. Suzuki President Toshihiro Suzuki credits the company’s decades of building Japanese mini vehicles for its ability to provide a genuinely usable cabin in such a small footprint.

For decades, European brands had most of this business to themselves. If you wanted an inexpensive car that could squeeze down a narrow street, Fiat would happily sell you a Panda, Renault a Twingo and Volkswagen an Up. Chinese automakers see an opening as those buyers go electric.

Leapmotor brought the T03 to Europe through its partnership with Stellantis, while BYD adapted its Chinese-market Seagull for Europe and called it the Dolphin Surf. Driving the latter, what stood out to me was how well it drove, how little felt cheap, and how much kit it had for its sub-€20,000 starting price.

By the time the Ignis arrives next year, European buyers will have had plenty of practice shopping for small EVs. Renault has revived both the 5 and the Twingo as electric cars, and there’s also the related Dacia Spring. Volkswagen has the ID. Polo, Cupra has the Raval, and Skoda has the Epiq, and there definitely seems to be demand for them. In September, a major VW dealer group reported more than 30,000 orders for the ID. Polo and a waiting list stretching to ten months.

That leaves one big question for the little Suzuki. What will it cost? Consider the redesigned Dacia Spring. Dacia moved production from China to Slovenia, shared the electric Twingo’s underpinnings, and produced a car that starts at €17,900 in Italy. It gets up to 155 miles (250 kilometers) of WLTP range from a battery only slightly larger than the one in the Ignis.

#4382. One More Than GT40: The Ford GT41 Le Mans Hypercar Is Finally Here

Yes, it’s about 41 inches tall. But that’s not really why it bears that name.

Ford’s return to the top class of the 24 Hours of Le Mans was finally unveiled during the Thanksgiving Day NFL game between the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, along with an official name that clearly evokes the company’s past success: GT41.

Of course, there weren’t 39 cars before the GT40, as that name comes from the fact that the car was 40 inches tall. The GT41, for what it’s worth is 41 inches tall… almost. Technically, the car is 41.7 inches from the ground to the top of its air intake, a dimension dictated by the current FIA regulations for the LMDh class. But GT42 doesn’t quite have the same ring to it.

And while the GT41 is based off the same Oreca chassis as used by the Genesis GMR-001 and outgoing Alpine A424 and Acura ARX-06, the car and team is a wholly internal Ford effort. “Everything that we’re building, it’s in-house,” said Mark Rushbrook, global director of Ford Racing, “It's the design, the engineering, the development, all the technical elements of the car.”

That internal approach particularly applies to the engine, which Rushbrook calls the heart of the car. The naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V-8 is based off Ford’s production engines, so much so that the block is shared with the supercharged 5.2-liter in the Mustang Dark Horse SC and F-150 Raptor R and is pulled straight from the line at the Essex Engine Plant in Windsor, Ontario. Assembled inside Ford’s dyno lab at the company’s headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, every part inside the racing engine “is designed by a Ford engineer,” according to Joseph Hendrickson, motorsports powertrain calibration engineer. “The engines are also tested on a dynamometer inside the same building. It’s a huge point of pride for us,” he said.

The final livery of the GT41 that will race at Le Mans will be revealed closer to the start of the 2027 WEC calendar, which being at Qatar in March. The car seen here features a camouflage pattern made of the Ford Racing wordmark, with Easter eggs hidden throughout that reflect the team’s pride as an American and Detroit-based automaker; look closely, and you’ll see an American flag, a bald eagle head, the Statue of Liberty, the Spirit of Detroit, and a football.

Until then, testing of the GT41 continues at several tracks around the world (and, as a reminder, Ford has no plans to run in IMSA or the 24 Hours of Daytona in 2027), while its new “Go Like Hell” ad campaign—directed by Zac Snyder and narrated by Matt Damon—will make regular appearances on your various screens for the rest of the year. Including this one, if you click on the video below.

#4380. Used Tesla Cybertruck prices jump after Musk kills it, one asks $150K

Used Cybertruck prices are up 10 to 15% in the month since Tesla announced it would end production of its electric pickup, according to listing data from CarGurus and Visor.

Some dealers are pushing it much further. One in New Jersey now wants $150,790 for a used Cyberbeast, about $36,000 more than Tesla charges for a brand-new one.

CarGurus’ price index puts the average used Cybertruck at $89,715, up 9.84% over the last 30 days and 13.5% over 90 days. Over the same 30 days, the broader used car market went down 1.37%.

Visor, which tracks dealer listings hourly and compares the same trucks month to month, shows a bigger move: +15% like-for-like versus last month, with an average asking price of $101,784 across 171 used trucks. Listings that sold in the last 30 days took 17 days on average.

The curve on CarGurus’ chart is flat at around $80,000 from July to late October. Then it bends up in November.

That lines up exactly with Tesla’s moves. On November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas, and Tesla raised prices by up to 10% the same day. A week later, Tesla stopped selling every Cybertruck except the Cyberbeast at $109,990. And this week, it bumped the Cyberbeast again to $114,990, which is what Tesla’s configurator shows today.

In early August, the cheapest Cybertruck you could order was $69,990. Now it’s $114,990.

Sorting CarGurus’ nationwide used Cybertruck inventory by price, the top listing is a 2026 Cyberbeast with 4,493 miles at J&S AutoHaus in Ewing, New Jersey. The asking price is $150,790 with fees.

CarGurus flags it as “Overpriced” and says it’s $35,773 above market. But the price history is the best part.

The dealer listed it at $134,995 on November 20. It went to $139,995 on November 25, the day after Tesla’s latest $5,000 Cyberbeast hike, and then to $149,995 the next day. That’s $15,000 in six days on a truck nobody has saved yet, according to CarGurus.

The same dealer also has a 2026 Cyberbeast with 851 miles at $145,790. Elsewhere, a 2024 Cyberbeast with 302 miles in Calumet City, Illinois, is listed at $148,816. And a 2024 dual-motor AWD with 1,500 miles in Lincoln, Nebraska, is at $145,306. That’s more than the $99,990 Tesla charged for a fully loaded Foundation Series AWD back in 2024.

Canadian dealers are playing the same game. The most expensive listing on AutoTrader.ca right now is a 2024 Cyberbeast with 1 km in Mississauga at C$199,999. The other 13 priced listings in the country sit between C$105,000 and C$141,995.

Sort the same CarGurus inventory from the bottom, though, and the picture changes.

A 2025 AWD with 22,495 miles is listed at $68,619 in San Bernardino, California. A 2024 Cyberbeast with 65,482 miles is at $70,118. There are several 2024 AWD trucks with 20,000 to 40,000 miles in the $77,000 to $80,000 range, and CarGurus rates many of them as good or great deals.

So the floor didn’t move all that much. What moved is the top and the middle.

There’s another detail in the CarGurus data. The 2024 model year is up 11.68% in 30 days, to $91,220. The 2025 model year is flat at $80,979, with 0% change over the same period.

The 2024 trucks include the Foundation Series, which came with Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” package bought outright. Tesla now only sells FSD as a subscription, so those trucks have something new ones don’t. The 2025s, mostly the cheaper AWD trims, aren’t getting the same bump.

It’s good news for current owners who want out. Many of them watched their trucks lose about half their value between 2024 and 2025. This is the best window they’ve had in a long time.

Um no. ASKING prices are up. Transaction prices? They will resume their cratering momentarily.

But we wouldn’t read it as a sudden wave of love for the Cybertruck. Tesla made the cheaper versions impossible to order, so used trucks are now the only way to get anything other than a $115,000 Cyberbeast. That pushes the middle of the market up. And part of it is just dealers testing what people will pay. These are asking prices.

The bigger question is what happens after production ends. Parts and service for a low-volume stainless-steel truck that Tesla no longer makes. We’d expect that to weigh on used values far more than a configurator price hike helps them.

If you own one and you’ve been thinking about selling, now looks like a good time. If you’re buying, don’t pay discontinuation hype prices.

#4379. Ionna Slashes EV Charging Prices For Thanksgiving

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Ionna, the EV charging network that ranked first in J.D. Power’s latest public charging satisfaction survey, has slashed prices at its stations across the country for Thanksgiving weekend.

The company, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States. That’s a 50% discount, and drivers don’t have to do anything special to get it—just plug in and pay, either through the automaker’s official smartphone app, the on-site payment terminals, or the Presto app for Tesla owners who want to enjoy the Autocharge function.

For long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a big difference. A single 50-kilowatt-hour session that used to cost $20 will now be just $10 plus tax, but seeing how many people are traveling across the country these days, multiple sessions will be necessary, driving the cost savings even further.

And it’s not like the cost reduction comes with any strings attached. Ionna uses 400-kilowatt chargers from Alpitronic exclusively, so there’s plenty of wiggle room for even the most power-hungry EVs out there. What’s more, many stalls have dual cords for each port, with a CCS connector and a NACS connector, so charging adapters aren’t needed at most locations.

Separately, Ionna has discounts for several automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, BMW, General Motors, and Stellantis.

The charging operator installed its first stalls in 2024, and it has wasted no time expanding its footprint quickly. On its second anniversary, Ionna celebrated by opening its 100th site, and the company now has 229 sites and nearly 1,900 ports nationwide, according to the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC). Still, the charging network is not slowing down, with dozens of locations under construction and plans to introduce 500-kW chargers in the near future.

Most EV brands support Plug & Charge at Ionna, with Tesla recently getting Autocharge functionality through a third-party smartphone application. Ionna itself doesn’t have a smartphone app, instead relying on automakers and third-party apps to integrate its locations. So far, this approach has turned out to be quite successful, with J.D. Power’s latest public charging survey putting the operator first, ahead of Tesla and the rest of the competition.

#4378. Driven: 2028 Porsche 718 Boxster EV Prototype Wags Its Tail Like a Mid-Engine Sports Car

The Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution, which is unusual for an EV, makes it handle like a sports car should.

There’s still a lot that Porsche won’t divulge about its forthcoming 2028 718 Boxster EV, including horsepower, battery capacity, range, pricing, or even its final, un-camouflaged looks. But after some seat time around the handling course at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles, we now know what it feels like at—and a little bit beyond—its cornering limits.

Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle.

In other words, this new EV feels like a mid-engine Boxster, because that’s where the weight is concentrated. Other than some hypercars, such as the Rimac Nevera, the forthcoming electric Boxster rides atop one of the first EV platforms built around a two-seat sports car. The 800-volt battery pack lives entirely behind the passenger cabin, in the place the engine used to reside, which leads to a 40/60 front/rear weight distribution, similar to the gas-powered Boxster’s 45/55 split. And since there’s no battery under the floor, you sit as low as you would in any other sports car.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 95648

We drove what will become the top Boxster model when it goes on sale after its formal debut in early 2027, but Porsche wouldn’t confirm what it will be called. S? GTS? These models wear Pirelli P Zero R Elect tires—and for the first time—mount on staggered-diameter wheels just like the latest 911. The tires measure 255/35ZR-20 up front and 305/30ZR-21 in back, which is more meat than even the last 718 Spyder RS. The company isn’t saying how much power this Boxster’s single rear motor will make—all electric Boxsters will be rear-drive only—but they do claim the sprint to 60 mph will require less than 3.0 seconds. After experiencing being pinned to the seat by a few launch-control starts, the new Boxster feels every bit that quick.

Porsche says this will be the quickest, most powerful Boxster with the highest cornering and braking performance, with a center of gravity that’s—no surprise—much lower than before. We can attest to feeling tons of grip, but can we feel the EV’s added weight? As the Boxster slithered through transitions and dove into apexes, we can’t say it felt heavy, although the squealing from its wide tires sounded at times more tortured than those we recall from the just-over-3000-pound gas-powered Boxster. Porsche says the Boxster EV’s curb weight will fall somewhere within that of the 911 lineup, which ranges from the 3350-pound Carrera to the 4000-pound Turbo S Cabriolet. Here’s hoping it’s toward the lower end of that range, which would be very light for an EV.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 95648

While this new electric version looks like a Boxster and the low seating position feels like a Boxster, with a forward view of a quickly disappearing hood, Porsche wanted to add some more nostalgic tie-ins by way of fabricated engine noises and simulated shifts. The Taycan got a similar E-Shift feature earlier this year, but while the Taycan’s engine noises weren’t modeled after a specific engine, the Boxster’s very much pays homage to its past. The Boxster’s E-Shift, which is controlled by a knob on the steering wheel and can shift automatically or be controlled by steering wheel paddles, mimics the 981 Boxster GTS’s 3.4-liter flat-six, which Porsche engineers say is the high-water mark for flat-six wails. They told us emissions compromises to the most recent flat-sixes made them choose that one from circa 2015. That said, there’s a bit of revisionist history going on with the electric Boxster’s 8000-rpm “redline” versus the actual 7600-rpm redline in its 981 muse. Either way, the noise emanating from the two speakers—one inside the cabin, one outside—absolutely sounds like a flat-six.

Although the synthesized sound is a solid re-creation, we do think it would be easy to identify the real from the facsimile in a blindfolded test. There’s a lot of nuance going on in the sounds of a flat-six belting to redline—intake and exhaust noise, valve and other mechanical clatter—and it’s hard to generate all of that from a couple speakers. That said, after doing a few hot laps with the system on, we believe it adds to the experience, and it felt weird to switch over to silent and shift-free lapping. We think we’d use this more in a sports car like the Boxster than in the four-door Taycan sedan.

What else did we learn? As before, the 983 Boxster has both front and rear trunks, and its NACS charge port, which is hidden behind a powered door in the middle of the rear bumper, is the first from Porsche to accommodate both AC and DC charging. Today’s Cayenne and Taycan electrics have separate ports for AC and DC with the NACS only handling DC charging.

Officially, there won’t be any gas-powered Boxster variants, but who knows what the lifecycle might hold, especially if early sales disappoint. After all, remember when the previous generation went four-cylinder only, but then the flat-six made a reappearance a few years later? While we’re as sad as anyone to see the flat-six and manual transmission leave the Boxster lineup, we think that anyone who drives the new one will agree it’s a great-handling sports car.

#4377. Tested: The 2028 Volvo XC60 T8 Is the Rangiest Plug-In Hybrid

Volvo’s aging middleweight SUV is a surprisingly strong performance contender with its revised powertrain.

On the journey to the future of automotive propulsion, Volvo was an early adopter of the all-electric ethos. The Swedish automaker initially vowed to stop selling all gasoline-powered cars—including hybrids—by 2030. A few years and three new all-electric models later, Volvo has radically altered that plan and will continue to sell hybrid models past that point. That includes extending the life of the existing lineup, with the already-near-decade-old second-gen XC60 getting a new T8 powertrain, which gives it the longest pure electric range of any plug-in hybrid on sale in the U.S.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

We have always appreciated the charms of the current-generation XC60, with a substantial package of changes sharpening its case for a few more years. Visually, the most obvious changes are a new front end incorporating LED matrix headlights and smaller revisions at the rear. The technical highlight is an improved 78-mile EPA electric range from a mammoth 37.9-kWh battery pack, this delivered to a motor on the rear axle; a smaller starter-generator can add modest assistance at the front as well. Volvo quotes a peak electric output of 208 hp, with the 2.0-liter turbo four that drives the front wheels able to deliver 247 horses. Inside, the XC60 receives small material and trim adjustments.

Engine: 1969-cc turbocharged inline-four, hybridized

Transmission: eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

As I pulled into Copenhagen’s morning traffic, Volvo’s Pure drive mode, which idles the gasoline-powered engine in favor of an all-electric experience, felt prudent among the multitude of commuting bicyclists. Silent running was entirely suited to the Scandinavian environment, but the XC60 T8 wasn’t stumbling over itself either when running under electrical power, Volvo having significantly juiced up the electric motor alongside the bigger battery pack.

While 208 hp in Pure EV mode has to work against 4855 pounds of weight, the T8 felt well suited to both metropolitan driving and the open road, the effective surge of electrical power proving itself on highways and the 9.9-mile-long Øresund Link that connects Denmark to Malmö, Sweden. Power delivery definitely wasn’t as aggressive as that of a spicy EV, but it wasn’t gentle either, and the electric motor had enough punch to drive the XC60 without me yearning for the gas engine to intervene. Something that won’t happen unless the accelerator is pushed to a kickdown position or by switching drive modes. The 78-mile EPA range is genuinely class-leading, and selecting the T8’s Charge mode rapidly replenished e-miles when selected.

Switching from the Pure to Hybrid mode was where the real fun began. And fun isn’t too strong a word for the unlikely performance of the split hybrid system as the 2.0-liter turbo adds its contribution to the front axle, giving a combined peak of 455 hp and what Volvo claims is 4.5-second 0–60-mph capability. In practice, the XC60 T8 felt shockingly quick, rapidly spinning up the speedometer at wide-open throttle. The accelerator has a two-part action, with softer response at the top of its travel metering electrical power before the combustion horses arrive with a suddenness. This was fun, but the transition also felt a bit too obvious considering how subtle some hybrids now are. Switching it up to Power mode refocused the powertrain by keeping the engine running and solved the on-and-off drama. The eight-speed automatic transmission shifts without drama, and there’s enough electrical torque that I didn’t even want for the missing steering-wheel paddle shifters.

We liked the way the pre-facelift XC60 T8 drove, and the new version impressed as much. Volvos are traditionally heavy and somewhat leisurely to respond, but the XC60 successfully belied its scale with impressively neutral handling on narrow Swedish country roads. My XC60 test vehicle was fitted with the optional air suspension and active shock absorbers, fighting body roll and delivering a reactive front end.

Similarly, Volvo’s power-steering system was smooth and direct, though both weight settings skewed overly light for my tastes. It’s not as overtly sporty as some performance SUVs, but its combination of qualities was definitely appealing. My only complaints were a somewhat agricultural soundtrack under full throttle and what was often a harsh ride over rough surfaces, bumps, and imperfections being transferred into the cabin.

I didn’t get a chance to plug in the XC60, but Volvo said the 2028 model can charge at speeds up to 7.2 kWh. All told, the XC60 PHEV will take around 5.7 hours to fully charge up at maximum speed.

Volvo has long succeeded at creating minimalist cabins without them looking sparse or cheap, and the XC60 continues to carry that torch with a few exceptions. And one of these exceptions was the 11.2-inch center touchscreen, which has been blown out of the casing found on previous model years to take over the entire console.

Annoyingly, climate-control functions are integrated into this display with multiple menus required for adjustment, the Android Auto software beneath it starting to show its age. Similarly, Apple CarPlay is only available through a wired connection—that’s so 2017. That said, the infotainment system was easy to operate despite its limitations. Plus, Volvo has perfected the art of displaying turn-by-turn directions on the instrument cluster; a dial speedometer and tachometer sit opposite each other with an appropriately scaled navigation map centered in between.

Beyond the technology, the XC60’s interior was a charming place to spend time. New Scandinavian-inspired materials on the dashboard included brushed wood and knit fabric, which looked upmarket and were pleasing to the touch. The light leather seats were firm yet comfortable and included massage, heating, and cooling functions, which can be operated all at once. Other notable interior design wins include a wooden sliding cup-holder cover, an alluring crystal shift knob, and satisfying brushed steel door handles. The Bowers & Wilkins stereo system on my test car was fantastic, and Volvo deserves points for retaining a traditional volume knob, as well as tactile buttons to skip songs.

If you want a properly long-range plug-in hybrid SUV, the Volvo XC60 may be your best option, at least for now. The next longest-range mid-size luxury SUV option is the Mercedes-Benz GLC Hybrid, which offers 54 all-electric miles. Toyota also offers a RAV4 Plug-In Hybrid with 52 miles of range. Volvo has not announced finalized U.S. pricing for the 2028 XC60 T8 yet.

Volvo interiors are well known for minimalist luxury, but even the Swedes can’t help themselves from including an easter egg here and there. Placed on the right edge of the passenger-side dashboard, Volvo has engraved a miniature Swedish flag on the brushed aluminum trim.

#4376. Toyota confirms the Highlander 9X will launch as its first EREV with top-tier tech in early 2027

The Toyota Highlander 9X will go on sale in early 2027 as the brand’s first extended-range electric vehicle with advanced new tech from Huawei and CATL.

Toyota joins Hyundai Motor Group, including Kia and Genesis, Ford, Volkswagen, and several other major OEMs with plans to launch its first EREV in the first quarter of 2027.

Toyota’s Chinese joint venture, GAC Toyota, announced at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27 that the EREV will use its flagship SUV nameplate, the Highlander 9X, when it arrives.

The Highlander 9X will blend Toyota’s classic global car heritage with some of China’s most advanced technology.

At the event, GAC Toyota revealed that the flagship EREV will use a battery custom-developed through its partnership with CATL, along with Huawei’s advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) and smart cockpit setup.

The EREV will be Toyota’s fifth “electrified” vehicle, joining battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), hybrids (HEVs), and fuel-cell electric vehicles (FCEVs).

Unlike fully electric vehicles, EREVs have a small gas engine that acts as a generator to charge the battery when it gets low, extending driving range.

According to Nikkei, Toyota aims to produce 200,000 EREVs in China in 2027, and about 400,000 units in 2028.

We will have to wait until closer to launch for battery and powertrain specifics, but local reports suggest Toyota’s EREV will deliver a combined CTLC range of over 621 miles (1,000 km) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

You can catch a glimpse of what appears to be the extended-range vehicle in the video GAC Toyota posted confirming the new EREV tech.

Since the Highlander 9X will be built in China, Toyota will not sell the EREV in the US. Instead, it will launch the fully electric Highlander BEV in the US in 2027.

The all-electric Toyota Highlander BEV will be available with front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive powertrains with two battery packs: 77 kWh or 95.8 kWh. The smaller (77 kWh) battery provides up to 287 miles of EPA-estimated range, while the larger (95.8 kWh) battery provides up to 320 miles in FWD models.

Like the outgoing version, the fifth-generation electric Toyota Highlander will offer three rows of seating and space for seven passengers.

#4375. Volvo Is Bringing Humanoid Robots Into Its Factories. Here's When They'll Start Working

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.

To make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are currently training them to do various tasks. Volvo said that it aims to support employees in repetitive and “ergonomically challenging work,” and it’s not the only car company that’s leaning towards replacing humans with robots.

Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories

While fixed robotic arms have been a staple of automotive factories for decades, some brands are now investing a lot of time and money in artificial intelligence-powered robots that can do tasks where components don’t always land in the same exact spot. So-called pick-and-place jobs are gradually being taken over by robots, with Tesla, General Motors, Ford, and Rivian slowly but surely filling their factories with complex robots.

Volvo is no different, and while the first humanoids shipped to the company’s plant in Ghent are only being trained right now, they’ll gradually start going to work in real conditions starting in mid 2027, the Swedish manufacturer said.

Currently, Volvo Cars is using imitation learning to teach the robot how to pick up and place certain components into two fixtures with high precision. Through the learning process, the team will gradually make the work more challenging, adding multiple parts, moving around the production area, and interacting with the plant’s automated systems.

“Aeon’s humanoid design means it can fit into our production as it is today, alongside our teams and existing automation,” says Magnus Nilsson, Chief Manufacturing Officer at Volvo Cars. “Our aim is for humanoid robots to take on some of the most physically demanding tasks and help make work more ergonomic for our people.”

The robot chosen by Volvo looks like a human, but it doesn’t have feet. Instead, the 5.4-foot (1.65-meter) robot moves on wheels and is capable of reaching up to 5.3 miles per hour (8.6 kilometers per hour). It weighs 132 pounds (60 kilograms) and can carry up to 22 lbs (10 kg). Several cameras and sensors are used to capture its surroundings and handle parts with precision.

#4374. New York Bans Post-Purchase Subscriptions on Vehicles

Monthly payments for heated seats? Not in the state of New York.

Are you paying a subscription fee for hardware already installed on your car? Not for much longer, you’re not. At least, not if you live in New York. Governor Kathy Hochul just signed a bill prohibiting automakers, dealers, and other third parties from charging subscription fees for vehicle features that use pre-installed components or hardware. Those heated seats you’re paying for? Get ready to cancel that subscription. That remote start you buy each winter? Treat yourself to an expensive latte from that cafe you like instead.

See all results for used cars for sale near 94043

The new law (S.9348A/A.10411A) doesn’t stop automakers from charging subscriptions entirely, but it does stop them from being able to charge recurring payments for hardware that doesn’t cause them any recurring costs.

Hochul’s office specifically pointed to heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving, and entertainment options. Heated seats are pretty cut and dry, but hands-free driving poses an interesting question. Systems such as Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD), GM’s Super Cruise, and Ford’s Blue Cruise all require customers to pay for a subscription to operate. All three systems work with the hardware installed on their respective vehicles, but the automakers could—and likely will—argue that they have recurring costs to keep the systems updated and safe.

Car and Driver reached out to Governor Hochul’s office for clarification on how the law will affect hands-free driving systems. We will update this story if we hear back. Meanwhile, the new law will go into effect on February 27, 2027, giving automakers and third-party companies time to enter into compliance.

#4373. TVR Returns From The Dead. Again

The moribund British sports car brand is back and wants to build the new Griffith at Lotus's factory.

Would you wait a decade for a new car? That’s the situation for anybody who raised their hand to buy the TVR Griffith when it was announced as far back as 2017. R&T’s own interest in the story faded soon after the reborn British brand announced the car was going to be heavily delayed. But, in truth, nobody realized how long the wait would be.

Delays were reportedly caused by the failure to secure funding to build a factory in Wales among other crises. It’s fair to say that the interest of most onlookers, and surely all of the potential buyers , faded as the excuses piled up. But after a change in ownership last year, TVR's new parent MOTV Group has announced that the Griffith will be produced at the Lotus factory in Hethel, with the first customer deliveries “planned for 2028,” although those likely restricted to buyers in the U.K.

There isn’t room for any detailed history of TVR here, but the original incarnation of the sport car maker collapsed into bankruptcy in 2006, having become both famous and infamous for brutish, fiber-bodied models including the 1990 Griffith, 1996 Cerbera and 1999 Tuscan Speed Six. Also the semi-mythical, one-of-one Speed 12 which was a star of early Gran Turismo games. TVR was reborn in 2013 after software entrepreneur Les Edgar bought the rights to the brand; according to public records in the U.K., Edgar resigned from the company board earlier this month.

MOTV Group was previously known as Charge Holdings, with subsidiary Charge Cars planning to build an electrified restomod version of the 1967 Ford Mustang before it, too, collapsed into bankruptcy. In 2025, Charge was saved by a group of investors and subsequently merged with TVR.

The official announcement of TVR’s latest return was accompanied by an image of what appears to be the 2017 concept car, now wrapped in a new disguise. Comparison of the images shows the same headlight position, panel lines, side-exit exhaust and identically patterned wheels. MOTV says the car will have a spaceframe chassis, a composite body, a V-8 engine with a manual transmission, and rear-wheel drive - all details aligning the 2017 version.

The original plan was for the new Griffith to use the iStream production process created by Gordon Murray’s then technology company, but this subsidiary has since been sold to ForSeven, which subsequently acquired McLaren Automotive which presumably owns the rights. So It will be interesting to discover if this technology-sharing partnership remains in place. Similarly, there is no confirmation that Cosworth is still involved in fettling the Ford Coyote V-8 that was meant to power the car as was originally announced.

Beyond the above facts the official announcement was short on details beyond naming the senior executive team, these including CEO Paul Abercrombie and CTO Steve MacManus, who was formerly an engineering vice president at Tesla and who seems to have worked on the aborted Apple car project.

Can TVR manage it this time? Given the soap opera of the brand’s recent history, there remains a substantial question mark over that one. As does the more relevant unknown for most R&T readers as to whether there is any chance a reborn Griffith would ever reach the U.S. It would be fun if it did, but let’s not get our hopes up yet.

In the U.K. he held senior staff positions with CAR, Autocar and evo, and in the U.S. he wrote for MPH and Autoweek before becoming Car and Driver’s European Editor for ten years. #4372. Prevost unveils Electric coach bus: 600 hp, 540 kWh, 250-mile range

Prevost, the Quebec coach builder owned by Volvo Group, has unveiled the H3-45 Electric, its first battery-electric motorcoach. It gets a 540 kWh Volvo battery, 450 kW (600 hp) from two electric motors, and both CCS1 and MCS charging as standard.

The H3-45 is Prevost’s flagship and one of the most common highway coaches in North America. Prevost is pitching the electric version as the same coach drivers and technicians already know, with a different powertrain.

Prevost first committed to an electric coach back in April 2022, when it announced a five-year electrification program backed by the Quebec government. That plan included a 100% electric coach and a retrofit kit to convert existing diesel coaches. The coach is now here. Prevost hasn’t said anything new about the retrofit kit.

Everything that moves the coach comes from Volvo. Prevost’s product page describes a single drive unit that combines two electric motors, an 8-speed automated manual transmission, and an oil retarder, rated at 450 kW (600 hp). Prevost’s tagline for it is “more power than diesel.”

The gearbox is the interesting part. Volvo’s own BZR Electric coach chassis in Europe uses a 2-speed automated transmission, but a 45-foot North American coach spends most of its life at highway speed and on long grades, and more gears help keep the motors in their efficient range. Prevost claims 97% motor efficiency across the working range, and drivers get adjustable regenerative braking for descents.

The battery system is made of six Volvo Cube2 units on a 600V architecture, for 540 kWh of total capacity. The brochure specifies 459 kWh of usable energy “across the full battery life,” so Prevost is holding back about 15% as a buffer.

The packs are liquid-cooled and IP6K9K-rated, and they use the same VCS2B coolant as the diesel H3-45. Volvo also backs every battery for refurbishment, second life, or recycling.

Prevost rates the coach at “up to 250 miles (400 km)” of range. But the footnote under that number says typical energy use runs up to 2.25 kWh per mile (1.40 kWh/km).

Do the math with Prevost’s own figures: 459 kWh of usable energy at 2.25 kWh/mile is about 204 miles, or roughly 328 km. Reaching 250 miles requires averaging about 1.84 kWh/mile. So 250 miles is the best case, and operators should plan around closer to 200 miles before keeping any reserve for the return to the depot.

Also, an energy buffer of almost 80 kWh is quite massive.

On a CCS1 charger at up to 350 kW, a 20-80% charge takes about 55 minutes, according to Prevost. The Megawatt Charging System (MCS) cuts that to about 35 minutes. The charge port is positioned for pull-through truck-stop stalls, and Prevost says no adapter is needed on public networks.

Those numbers also tell you how fast MCS actually charges this coach. Going from 20% to 80% of 459 kWh means adding about 275 kWh. Doing that in 35 minutes averages roughly 470 kW. That’s a lot faster than CCS1, but nowhere near a megawatt.

The value of MCS here is access as much as speed. Megawatt chargers are being built for electric semi trucks, like the first MCS truck charge in North America at EV Realty’s San Bernardino hub, and newer dispensers like Kempower’s dual CCS and MCS charger serve both connectors. A coach that can pull into those stalls has a lot more charging options on the highway.

The rest of the spec sheet reads like a regular H3-45: up to 52 passengers, Cloud One Premium seating, Prevost Driver Assist, LED headlights, five monitors, automatic tag-axle unload, and a kneeling system. 360-degree cameras and a winter package are optional.

Prevost markets the coach as a certified zero-emission vehicle and leans hard on grant eligibility in its brochure. There’s one catch in the fine print. The optional cold-weather heater is diesel-fired, and it produces emissions when it runs. For Canadian and northern US operators, that’s probably the option most of them will tick.

Prevost didn’t include pricing or a delivery date in its announcement. Jay Menard, who runs Prevost’s ZEV programs, told Electric Autonomy that pilots start in early 2027 and that production deliveries should begin around mid-August 2027.

Prevost isn’t first here. Its main North American rival, MCI, unveiled its J4500 CHARGE electric coach in 2021 with a 544 kWh battery and more than 200 miles of rated range. So Prevost is arriving about five years later with essentially the same battery size.

What Prevost brings is a single-OEM drivetrain from Volvo, more power, a multi-speed gearbox, and MCS. It also keeps the electric version on the same platform as the diesel H3-45. And Prevost confirmed in September that its 2027 Volvo D13 diesel meets the new EPA and CARB standards. The diesel H3-45 isn’t going anywhere.

#4371. Save Now, Pay Later: Why It Makes Sense to Buy a Less Expensive Old Car

Life is too short to wait for the perfect vehicle.

I have a bit of automotive ADHD. I can’t stick with a single car for too long. I get bored, reach my wit’s end with throwing money into it, or simply come across a good deal through my endless scouring of Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist. That means I’m constantly switching cars, and because of my limited wealth, those cars generally fall into the category I’d affectionately describe as shitboxes.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Look, I don’t want to buy shitboxes. It’s just the best course of action if I want to experience as many cars as possible for as reasonable a price as possible. Buying shitboxes is not for the faint of heart. Here’s how I do it and why.

When I’m searching for my next deal, I look for clean-title cars, ideally without fatal rust or debilitating powertrain issues. Pretty much every other problem—trivialities such as cosmetics and air-­conditioning—is acceptable. That mind-set is how I’ve proudly managed to own three different generations of BMW M5 and a 270,000-mile Lexus GX470 that I drove from New York to Alaska and back without issue. The shitbox mentality gets the job done, especially with Aughts enthusiast icons, which still offer modern convenience and potential reliability at the tail end of the depreciation curve.

Most recently­, I landed myself a 2009 Mercedes-­Benz G550 for about half off market value.

That story began on a slow Thursday afternoon, while I was letting the Marketplace algorithm feed me its best. The G550 popped up, and I offered the seller $3500 under asking. Instead of telling me to kick rocks, he wrote, “If you are serious huyer [sic] bring me cash today and it’s yours.” Guess what I did.

With payment cobbled together from my checking account and, to avoid the delay of a bank transfer, cash loans from a few friends who share my affliction, I drove five hours from New York through torrential rain and handed over the money in a dark lot in Northern Virginia late at night. It was sketchy and awesome. Now I own a G550 that’s stuck in second gear and has a sunroof flanked by worrisome rust holes.

Aside from paying less up front, if you buy a car at its floor, you’re only going to sell it for more. Probably. And when it comes to maintenance costs, I would rather cheap out on the purchase price, knowing what’s already broken, than drop double that on a better example and wait for something to inevitably break. Also, I could pay cash in full for the vehicle and then fix the issues I want to fix over time while enjoying what I’m able to enjoy about the car along the way. All with the assurance that whatever had to be fixed was completed under my supervision and done correctly. According to my shitbox math, it makes sense.

I turned 30 this summer. By a conservative estimate, I’ve owned at least 30 cars. But I’m not in the game of flipping. For me, it’s all about having as many adventures as I can behind the wheel of the greatest cars that have graced this world’s roads before they explode in value on Bring a Trailer’s auction pages. Holding out for perfection is not an option.

Road & Track’s digital director is often surrounded by beat-up project cars. His fleet currently consists of a problematic manual-swapped 1991 BMW 325i sedan and a Mercedes G550. Before R&T, Brown worked at Jalopnik, The Drive, and Business Insider.

#4370. Every Brand Selling Hybrid Vehicles in the U.S. for 2027

Hybrid car sales are at a high, and that means plenty of choices in segments including SUVs, sedans, vans, and sports cars.

For all the talk about electric vehicles over the past several years, the bigger story is the current hybrid wave. From 2024 until the end of September 2026, gas-electric hybrids soared from just over eight percent of new light-duty vehicle sales to 16 percent, or double the share of EVs, according to the Energy Information Administration. After consecutive years of parallel growth that saw battery-electric and gas-electric vehicles rise together starting in 2020, hybrid sales have never been higher while EVs, despite a spurt in 2025 and 2026, are not recovering.

This means that there’s now more choice than ever among hybrid vehicles: nearly every major automaker offers at least one hybrid model, and many of them offer a wide range of hybrids in various body styles from SUVs to sports cars and everything in between. Here’s a guide to all hybrids on sale, across all segments (excluding 48-volt hybrids that are not designed to power a vehicle solely with electric motors).

Every Brand Selling Sports Cars | Every Brand Selling EVs | Best-Looking Cars

Bentley makes the world’s only four-seat plug-in hybrid convertible, the Continental GTC. The ravishing powertrain, standard with 671 horsepower or 771 horsepower in the Speed and Mulliner, isn’t exclusive to the the Continental range, either. The twin-turbo V-8 and its 22-kWh battery pack are shared with the Flying Spur sedan, both of which claim 30 miles of electric range (we did 49 in the Continental). A turbo V-6 and an 18-kWh battery are found in the Bentayga Hybrid SUV.

BMW offers a sextet of plug-in hybrids that throw heavy punches under hard acceleration. The 550e, 750e, and X5 xDrive50e share a 483-hp setup with a turbo inline-six good for between 34 and 44 miles of electric range, while the M5, M5 Touring and XM electrify a twin-turbo V-8 for a total of 717 or 738 horsepower. We expect to see more hybrid setups on the high-performance end of the lineup in the future, although the next-gen M3 is also offering a fully electric variant, signifying a possible shift in BMW’s strategy.

Chevrolet’s sole hybrids are found within the Corvette lineup. The first is the Grand Sport X, which supplements the base Stingray’s 6.7-liter V-8 with a front electric motor for a total of 721 horsepower. The other is the ZR1X, which costs a quarter-million dollars and pumps 1250 horsepower from a turbo 5.5-liter V-8 and a front electric motor. It gets 12 mpg in the city and goes 225 mph. It’s beyond magnificent. Still, Chevy is planning more mainstream hybrids, as the three-row Traverse SUV is poised to get a hybrid variant in the future.

All mid-engine Ferraris come as hybrids—and 869 horsepower is the bare minimum. That’s the output from the twin-turbo flat-plane V-6 and axial-flux motor in the new 296 Speciale. The wedgy 849 Testarossa stuffs a twin-turbo V-8 and triple motors for 1036 horsepower. For $3.7 million, the almighty F80 goes backward in cylinder count (but with a more powerful twin-turbo V-6 and three motors) and forward with F1 tech for 1184 horsepower. Buy a front-engine Ferrari and you’ll have to settle for nonhybrid V-12s and V-8s.

Ford sold some of the industry’s first PHEVs in the 2010s—remember the Fusion Energi?—but no longer offers any hybrid sedans or SUVs. The Escape Hybrid and PHEV are gone. But one of our favorite hybrids on sale is the Maverick compact pickup, which can hit 40-plus mpg in the city with front- or all-wheel drive. The F-150 PowerBoost, which uses a twin-turbo V-6 with an electric motor, is more capable but not as smooth to drive as the Maverick.

The first Genesis hybrids aren’t launching until the 2028 model year in the U.S., but we decided to include them here anyway. The lineup includes the gorgeous G80 mid-size luxury sedan and the stately GV80 mid-size luxury SUV. Their hybrid powertrains both use turbo 2.5-liter inline-fours and represent the next stage of the Hyundai group’s hybrid expertise. The batteries now use liquid instead of air cooling, a seven-speed automatic replaces the six-speed, and the torque output (391 lb-ft) matches the twin-turbo V-6 in the 3.5T trims.

Honda has been into hybrids almost as long as Toyota has (see the 1999 Honda Insight), and the company’s current hybrid powertrain is a gem. With direct drive (no transmission), the two-motor, 2.0-liter inline-four setup is quick, efficient, and downright fun. It’s available on the CR-V, the Civic sedan and hatchback, and the Accord sedan, and it’s the only choice on the Prelude coupe.

While the Elantra Hybrid takes a hiatus until 2028, Hyundai’s next-best mileage champ is the Sonata Hybrid, which can surpass 50 mpg and offers generous rear leg room. Hyundai’s three compact and mid-size SUVs, including a new-gen Tucson, get hybrid versions and all offer all-wheel drive. Unlike many mainstream hybrids, Hyundai employs a six-speed automatic instead of a CVT or direct drive. The Tucson plug-in hybrid is no longer available.

While Jeep axed the plug-in hybrid 4xe trims of the Wrangler and Grand Cherokee, an extended-range series hybrid is coming to the Grand Wagoneer with a whopping 647 horsepower. The hybrid-only Cherokee compact SUV comes with only 210 horsepower but up to an estimated 39 mpg city rating.

Like Hyundai, Kia’s diversity of gas, hybrid, and electric powertrains has paid off in spades in terms of sales. There are eight hybrids total in the Kia lineup, with plug-in hybrids available on the Sorento and Sportage (no longer on the Niro). Every SUV has a hybrid option, and so does the Carnival minivan.

Surprised to see Lamborghini peddling hybrids? The brand’s lineup is now entirely hybrid, actually, starting with the plug-in hybrid Urus SUV which comes in 789-hp SE and 801-hp Performante versions. Those SUVs can do an estimated 35 miles on electricity. The 907-hp Temerario is also a plug-in hybrid, offering a pitiful four miles of electric range. But the only hybrid that revs to 10,000 rpm. Then there’s the 1001-hp Revuelto and 1050-hp Revuelto SV which pair a giant V-12 with three electric motors. What a time to be alive.

Leave it to Lexus to combine big power with efficiency. This was the brand that in 2008 gave us the LS600hL, a hybrid flagship that could match the refinement from 12-cylinder German sedans. Now that we live in an SUV world, the LX700h is the modern equivalent—at up to $143,000, it’s the rare four-passenger hybrid SUV with four-wheel drive and a fully reclining rear seat. The TX500h is the next step down (the PHEV is gone for 2027). The RX and NX each offer three hybrid trims including plug-ins, while the new ES350h is now the sole hybrid sedan.

Lincoln moved away from hybrids only to come running back—and they took a long way home. The brand’s two hybrid SUVs, the compact Corsair and mid-size two-row Nautilus, are plucked straight from China, since Ford hasn’t yet carved out factory space for these models in North America. They enjoy a substantial exterior refresh for 2027, too. Each comes with turbo inline-fours and all-wheel drive, while the Nautilus goes screen crazy with a 48-inch display hugging the bottom of the windshield.

While the CX-50 Hybrid uses a Toyota-based powertrain, the CX-90 Hybrid is all Mazda. It’s a nicely styled three-row plug-in hybrid SUV with an estimated 25 miles of electric range. The two-row CX-70 Hybrid is discontinued, but there’s a CX-5 Hybrid on the horizon, though it may not arrive until 2028.

Want a Le Mans racer as a comfortable supercar? There’s no better choice than a McLaren Artura, which has a howling twin-turbo V-6 that has the party trick of leaving and arriving in complete silence. With 11 miles of estimated electric range, it can go nearly three times as far on a charge than a Lamborghini Temerario can. The combined 690 horsepower and McLaren’s light-as-a-feather chassis are heavenly. Choose the coupe or a spider.

While AMG customers weren’t so enthusiastic about the C63 and its F1-derived four-cylinder plug-in hybrid powertrain, they’re happy plugging into turbo-sixes and turbo V-8s on the higher-end models. Every hybrid AMG is PHEV, whether it’s a sedan, wagon, SUV, convertible, or coupe. The E Performance trims of the SL and GT Coupe make more than 1000 pound-feet of torque.

Mercedes-Benz’s three hybrid models are all plug-in hybrids just like their AMG cousins, only less potent. The S580e is our personal favorite, as we were able to reach 58 miles of all-electric range on the highway, handily beating the factory estimate. The GLE500e also shares the same inline-six and delivers similar range, while the GLC350e has an inline-four. Like the AMGs, the GLE and S-class hybrids support DC fast charging, a rare feature on a PHEV.

Mitsubishi was first to market with a plug-in SUV, and it hasn’t really received due credit. Part of it is the premium price the Outlander PHEV commands and its so-so performance, though it’s updated for 2027 with more power. It also has plenty of features, decent interior quality, and a healthy 45-mile electric range. Along with the regular Outlander, it’s also the only three-row SUV in the compact segment.

As the only series hybrid in the mainstream segment, Nissan has made a big splash with the Rogue Hybrid after more than a decade without any gas-electric powertrain in its lineup. Think of the company’s e-Power hybrid setup like an extended-range EV where the gas engine serves only as a generator for the electric motors, but without the plug or the big battery. We like how it drives—a lot.

Porsche’s conventional hybrid powertrain sits in its most prized product, the 911, where the T-Hybrid installs one or two electric turbos and a small battery on the GTS and Turbo S. The models with the E-Hybrid badge are plug-in hybrids. The Panamera has three PHEV choices, including the Turbo’s V-8 powertrain shared with Bentley for up to 771 horsepower. The Cayenne Hybrid has either a V-6 hybrid setup or a similar V-8 setup in either the SUV or Coupe body style.

#4369. BYD’s flagship electric minivan debuts with a new style and 559 miles of range

BYD’s new flagship MPV is not your average minivan. The Whale can drive over 559 miles (900 km) on a single charge, charge in as little as five minutes, and it’s packed with BYD’s latest tech.

The Whale is the first flagship multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) from BYD’s Ocean series. BYD has several sub-brands, including Denza, Yangwang, and Fang Cheng Bao, and sells vehicles under two primary lineups: Ocean and Dynasty.

BYD unveiled the Whale for the first time at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27, with a launch set for the first quarter of 2027.

Measuring 5,270 mm long, 1,996 mm wide, and 1,815 mm tall, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase, BYD’s newest minivan is slightly longer than the Chrysler Pacifica.

The Whale will be available in both plug-in hybrid (PHEV) and pure electric (EV) powertrains. Both will use BYD’s latest Blade Batteries 2.0. The PHEV version will offer a pure-electric CLTC range of 248 miles (400 km), while the EV variant offers over 559 miles (900 km) of range on a single charge.

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric minivan can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes.

For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes only nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C(-22°F), it takes just 3 minutes longer, or 12 minutes total.

Leading up to its debut, camouflaged prototypes were spotted with a boxy design that looked closer to a traditional gas-powered MPV.

However, the Whale looks better than expected. It adopts BYD’s updated Ocean design with smooth edges and a double-layer staggered grille.

BYD didn’t reveal many details outside of confirming the name and showcasing the design. With LiDAR on the roof, the Whale will offer BYD’s latest Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS).

The Whale will go on sale in the first quarter of 2027, joining the Dynasty Series Xia, Linghui M9, and Denza D9 as BYD’s fourth MPV.

Prices will be revealed closer to launch, but the Whale is expected to start at around 300,000 yuan ($45,000), filling the gap between the Xia, which starts at 249,800 yuan ($37,500), and the Denza D9 at 359,800 yuan ($54,000).

#4368. A Used Cybertruck Is Selling A Month Faster Than A Ford F-150

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

If you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet. It’s America’s best-selling midsize truck and has a reputation for holding its value. Or you might pick the super frugal Ford Maverick Hybrid. But the truck that beat them both was the Tesla Cybertruck.

The data from the new iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla announced it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027. The study looked at one- to five-year-old vehicles and ranked models by how long they’d been listed before selling.

The Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall. The Maverick Hybrid came closest at 43.3 days, followed by the Rivian R1T at 45.2 and the F-150 Lightning at 47.4. The Tacoma came in fifth position.

The gap between the two electric pickups at either end of the list was even more striking. A used Chevrolet Silverado EV took 107.5 days to sell, putting it last among the 24 trucks in the study. That’s a 68-day difference between two American electric pickups. Across the wider used market, EVs averaged about 46 days to find a buyer, around nine fewer than hybrids and 15 fewer than gas vehicles.

How quickly a used Cybertruck sold seems to have changed a lot since May 2024, when some sellers were cutting as much as $30,000 from their asking prices after listing their trucks for close to $200,000. By December of that year, we reported that used Cybertrucks were piling up on dealer lots, with data at the time showing they stayed for 75 days, up from 27 in May.

Then owners got a look at what Tesla itself would pay for a used Cybertruck trade-in. One year later, in May 2025, one owner of a $99,990 dual-motor Foundation Series truck got a trade-in estimate of $65,400 after driving it just 6,211 miles.

So even though the Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used pickup in iSeeCars’ new study, it didn’t report what buyers paid, so we don’t know whether owners got their asking price or had to lower it to sell.

Tesla will build the last Cybertrucks at the end of summer 2027, and this will reshape their used market. Elon Musk originally announced production would end around the middle of the year, but then extended the run to fill more orders. And if you order a Cybertruck now, the only one you can get is the $110,000 tri-motor Cyberbeast, so anyone who wants a less expensive dual-motor truck has to look for a used example.

Once the last new Cybertruck is sold, I’d expect collectors and everyday truck buyers to look at used ones differently. Someone after a clean Foundation Series truck with low miles might pay a little extra for one close to home, especially since it could be months before another comes up for sale nearby.

At the same time, someone who just needs an electric pickup to tow a trailer has more options. If a used dual-motor Cybertruck costs about the same as a Ford F-150 Lightning or a Rivian R1T, I suspect that buyer will care more about mileage, condition, and how much battery warranty is left than when Tesla built its last truck.

#4367. Pay Now, Save Later: Why It Makes Sense to Buy a More Expensive Old Car

A clean used ride is both easier and cheaper to enjoy.

One of the problems with the classic end of the automotive hobby is that everyone wants a clean car. Whether your goal is to keep it that way, preserve and use it, or modify it to suit your tastes, the road will be a whole lot smoother if you start from a healthy place. Trust me, buying a good example of an older car is better for your health. I’ve been there.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Why would you buy something with obvious issues? To save money, right? But guess what—you’re undervaluing your own time, and, except for a few rare occasions, the savings never materialize. Trying to fix up a bad car without already being an expert bad-car fixer is like trying to treat someone with a spinal injury without being a doctor: It’s going to be brutal, painful, and expensive in ways you can’t anticipate.

A clean car has fewer unknowns. With a not-so-clean car, damage from accidents may not have been repaired to factory spec. Paintwork may not quite match. “Just a little bit of rust” is almost never an accurate assessment of that metal-eating menace. “You’re not going to believe what we found in here” will become your own sad catchphrase.

This is particularly true for Aughts-era cars because they are potentially usable for everyday driving. The fantasy of dailying something like a sweet E39 BMW M5 can run into the reality of owning a 20-something-year-old specialty product. You might be thinking: It’s not like buying an old Ford Woody and needing artisan-­level skills. Most Aughts cars should be reliable enough to drive regularly at freeway speeds. The worst that could happen is I might need to replace a few still readily available parts, right? Maybe. Maybe not. You’ll quickly find out which local shops won’t touch cars that are over 10 years old.

Now, if I were a talented hobbyist mechanic, or a professional one, I could probably spot a deal where my skill set could be applied to a particular car’s needs, creating unique value for me. And yes, anyone could learn those skills with some time and effort. But do you want to spend your nights and weekends wrenching, not to customize your car but to repair it? Or do you want to spend that time driving?

For everyone who does not fix cars for a hobby and wants a cool car to drive for fun and maybe modify a bit: Get the clean car. Time is money, and if your money has to buy professional time un-shitboxing a previous owner’s mistakes, it’s going to cost you both dollars and days. You’re not just losing what you may have saved on the purchase price in repairs but also paying in the lost opportunity of a car that’s not on the road being enjoyed.

One of my recent purchases is an old Mercedes that I am having professionals modify for me. The ­difference between a great and a rough example of this car is about $15,000. Real money, but to make a bad example into a good one would be more than ­double that figure.

So yeah, you pay more on the way in. But guess what? When you go to sell it, you’re on the other end of the same equation. Money out, money in. Because everybody wants the clean example, and you’re ­holding the goods.

Matt Farah is a lifelong car enthusiast who began his automotive career at dealerships, rental agencies, and detail shops before discovering the power of YouTube in 2006, with his channel The Smoking Tire.
